try: Pick one change you are postponing until later in life. Do a small piece of it this week.

title: Enemy of Jibril? He only brought what Allah sent.
subtitle: Blaming the messenger for the message
then: Ibn Jarir said scholars agree this was revealed when some said {trap}Jibril is our enemy, Mikail our friend.{/trap} Anas narrated that Abdullah bin Salam heard the Prophet ﷺ say Jibril told him the answers to three questions, then accepted Islam. {idea}Jibril brings nothing except by Allah's command.{/idea}
now: You do not like the imam, so you ignore the reminder he gave. You do not like your sister in law, so the true thing she said does not count. {trap}Disliking the carrier is an easy way out of the message.{/trap}
old: I cannot take that seriously, look who said it.
new: If the message is from Allah, my feelings about the carrier do not change it.
try: Think of a good reminder you dismissed because of who said it. Take one thing from it today.

title: You cannot pick and choose among Allah's angels and messengers.
subtitle: Enmity to one is enmity to all

row.title: I can love one and hate another

then: Jibril and Mikail are both named because some claimed one as enemy and the other as friend. Ibn Kathir: {idea}whoever takes one messenger as an enemy has taken them all as enemies,{/idea} since all are sent by Allah. He cites 22:75: Allah chooses messengers from angels and from people.
now: You love the verses about mercy and skip the ones about accountability. You quote one scholar you like and wave off another who is just as sound. {idea}Guidance comes as a whole.{/idea} Taking only the parts you like is choosing yourself over the Sender.
old: I accept the parts of the message that feel right to me.
new: The angels and messengers all serve one Lord. Accepting Him means accepting all of them.
try: Read one verse today on a topic you usually avoid. Sit with it without arguing.

title: The signs are clear. Only defiance denies them.
subtitle: When the problem is not the evidence
then: Ibn Jarir said the clear signs included the Quran telling the hidden details of earlier scriptures. Ibn Abbas: {idea}you recite this Book though you never read a book, and you tell them what is in theirs.{/idea} The verse says {trap}only the defiantly disobedient deny such signs.{/trap}
now: You ask for one more sign before you change. Then it comes, a scare at the clinic, a friend's sudden death, and you ask for another. {trap}At some point the question is not proof but will.{/trap}
old: If I had clearer proof, I would commit.
new: The signs are already clear. What I need is the will to act on them.
try: Name one sign Allah has already shown you. Act on it in one small way today.

title: Every promise made, some threw it away.
subtitle: A pattern of broken pledges
then: When reminded of their covenant about the Prophet ﷺ, Malik bin As-Sayf said Allah never took any pledge from them. Then this verse came. Al-Hasan Al-Basri said: {trap}they make a promise today and break it tomorrow.{/trap}
now: I will start praying properly after Eid. I will call my father this weekend. I will stop that habit from Monday. {trap}A promise you keep breaking becomes a pattern.{/trap} {idea}Small promises kept build a trustworthy heart.{/idea}
old: I meant it when I promised. Breaking it later is just life.
new: The promises I keep breaking say something about what I really believe.
try: Keep one small promise today, even one you made only to yourself.

title: The Book thrown behind their backs, as if unknown.
subtitle: Turning away from what you know

row.title: as if they did not know

then: As-Suddi said: when the Prophet ﷺ came, they wanted to argue using the Torah, but {idea}the Torah and the Quran agreed.{/idea} So they set the Torah aside and turned to books of magic. Qatadah: {trap}they knew the truth, abandoned it, and denied even having it.{/trap}
now: The Quran on your shelf, wrapped in cloth, high and safe, and untouched since Ramadan. Not rejected. Just behind your back. {idea}Bring it in front of you again, even for one page.{/idea}
old: I respect the Quran, I just do not have time to read it.
new: Keeping the Book out of sight is a quiet way of throwing it behind my back.
try: Take the Quran down today and read one page, with the translation if you need it.

title: They swapped the Book for magic that harms and never helps.
subtitle: Sulayman was innocent; the devils were not
then: As-Suddi narrated that devils mixed lies with stolen news and spread books of sorcery, then claimed {trap}Sulayman ruled by magic.{/trap} The verse clears him: {idea}Sulayman did not disbelieve, the devils did.{/idea} The two angels at Babylon warned anyone first: we are a trial, do not disbelieve.
now: Someone suggests a person who can fix your marriage or bind a rival. Or you spend nights on videos about curses and charms. {trap}It promises control and delivers fear.{/trap} {idea}Nothing harms you except by Allah's leave.{/idea}
old: There must be some hidden power that can fix this for me.
new: No one can harm me except by Allah's leave, so I turn to Him, not to secrets.
try: When you feel afraid of harm from others, make a sincere dua for protection and leave it with Allah.

title: Had they believed and been mindful, the reward was far better.
subtitle: The door that stayed open
then: After the warning about magic, the verse turns gently. {reward}If they had believed and feared Allah, the reward from Him would have been better,{/reward} if only they knew. {idea}The better trade was always available.{/idea}
now: The shortcut always looks faster: the bribe to speed up the papers, the charm to win the person, the lie to close the sale. {reward}The slow way with Allah pays more, and it is never too late to take it.{/reward}
old: Doing it the straight way means losing out.
new: What Allah gives for faith and mindfulness is better than any shortcut.
try: Choose the straight way in one situation today where a shortcut tempts you.

title: Drop the word that can be twisted. Use a clear one.
subtitle: Manners of speech with the Prophet ﷺ

row.title: Ra'ina
sub: could be twisted into an insult

row.title: Unzurna
sub: look at us, help us understand

row.title: choose words that cannot be bent

then: Some used the word {trap}ra'ina with a twist of the tongue as mockery,{/trap} as 4:46 describes. Some believers used it innocently. Allah told the believers to {idea}say unzurna instead, a clear word with no double meaning, and to listen.{/idea}
now: A joke in the family group chat with a hidden edge. A reply at work that sounds polite but stings. Or an innocent word you keep using that others hear as mockery. {idea}Respectful speech chooses words that cannot be bent.{/idea}
old: My words are fine as long as I mean them well.
new: Good manners include choosing words that cannot be twisted into disrespect.
try: Before you send your next message, reread it once for any double meaning.

title: Some do not want good to reach you. Allah chooses anyway.
subtitle: Mercy is not up for others' approval

row.title: what Allah wills
sub: His mercy to whom He chooses

then: The verse tells the early believers that some among the People of the Scripture and the idolaters {trap}did not want any good sent down to them from their Lord.{/trap} The answer: {idea}Allah chooses for His mercy whom He wills, and He is the owner of great bounty.{/idea}
now: The relative who hopes your business fails. The colleague who would rather you did not get the role. You feel their wish like a weight. {idea}Their wish has no say in Allah's mercy.{/idea} Keep doing good and leave the giving to Him.
old: If they are against me, my chances are ruined.
new: No one's ill wish can stop the mercy Allah has chosen for me.
try: When you notice someone's envy, make dua for yourself and for them, and carry on.

title: When Allah replaces a ruling, He brings one better or equal.
subtitle: Change in guidance is not a mistake

row.title: the Wise One chose the timing

then: Some objected that a true revelation could never change a ruling. The verse answers: {idea}whatever Allah abrogates, He brings something better or like it.{/idea} Ibn Abbas said better means more beneficial and easier for you. Ibn Kathir notes this applies to rulings, not to stories.
now: A doctor changes your child's medicine as she grows. A teacher moves you from easy drills to harder ones. Nobody calls that inconsistency. {idea}Allah, who knows us best, guided the first believers step by step.{/idea}
old: If a ruling changed, maybe the guidance was not certain.
new: Allah moved His servants from one ruling to a better one, with perfect timing.
try: Think of one way Allah has eased something in your life over time. Thank Him for it.

title: He owns the heavens and earth. You have no other protector.
subtitle: Whose decision it is
then: This verse continues the reply about changing rulings. Ibn Kathir: {idea}He alone owns His creation and does with it as He wills.{/idea} He gives health and illness, success and failure, and allows and forbids as He wills. {reward}Besides Him there is no protector and no helper.{/reward}
now: The visa is pending. The test results are not back. You refresh your email and call the friend who knows someone. All fine, but {idea}the One who owns the outcome is not in your phone.{/idea} He is closer.
old: If I pull enough strings, I can secure this.
new: Allah owns everything, so He is the protector I lean on first.
try: Before you call anyone about your worry today, make dua about it first.

title: Do not question your Messenger the way Musa was questioned.
subtitle: Questions that seek to escape, not to learn

row.title: to be difficult
sub: bring us a book from the sky

row.title: do what you can of it

then: Ibn Abbas said some challenged the Prophet ﷺ: {trap}bring us a book from heaven and make rivers flow, then we will believe.{/trap} The verse compares it to how Musa was questioned. When a man asked if Hajj was every year, the Prophet ﷺ said: {idea}leave me as I leave you. When I command you, do what you can.{/idea}
now: Before helping your neighbour you ask: is it obligatory? Does it count if? You want a ruling for every corner before taking one step. {idea}Some questions help you walk. Some are ways of standing still.{/idea}
old: I need every detail answered before I commit.
new: I can act on what is clear and stop hunting for reasons to delay.
try: Notice one question you keep asking to put off a good deed. Drop it and do the deed.

title: They wished to turn you back. Pardon and overlook.
subtitle: Meeting envy with patience

row.title: a wish to turn you back

then: The early believers in Madinah faced people who {trap}wished to turn them away from faith, out of envy,{/trap} even though the truth was clear to them. Allah told them to {idea}pardon and overlook until Allah brings His command.{/idea} Usamah bin Zayd said the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions forgave and were patient as told.
now: Someone mocks your hijab at work, or your fasting at a family dinner. A cousin keeps saying you have changed, you used to be fun. {idea}You do not have to win every exchange.{/idea} Patience is not weakness; it is trusting that Allah is able.
old: If I do not hit back, I will look weak.
new: Pardoning and overlooking, while trusting Allah, is strength.
try: Next time someone needles you about your faith, answer calmly or let it pass, and say a quiet dua.

title: Pray, give, and send good ahead. You will find it with Allah.
subtitle: What to do while you wait
then: Right after telling them to pardon and wait, Allah gives them something to do. {idea}Establish prayer, give zakah.{/idea} Ibn Kathir: Allah encouraged them to busy themselves with deeds that benefit them on the Day of Resurrection. {reward}Whatever good you send ahead, you will find it with Allah.{/reward}
now: Instead of replying to the troll for the fifth time, close the app and pray two rakahs. Instead of rehearsing the argument in your head, give something to the person collecting outside the mosque. {reward}Nothing you do for Allah is lost, He sees it.{/reward}
old: I have to deal with my critics before I can focus.
new: The best answer to hostility is to keep sending good deeds ahead.
try: Turn one moment of irritation today into two rakahs or a small charity.

title: Only we get into Paradise? Bring your proof.
subtitle: Wishful thinking about who is saved
then: Some said {trap}none will enter Paradise unless he is a Jew or a Christian.{/trap} Abu Al-Aliyah said these were wishes they hoped Allah would grant, with no basis. The Prophet ﷺ was told to answer: {idea}bring your proof, if you are truthful.{/idea}
now: We are from a religious family, so we are fine. Our mosque has the right way. Our group is the saved one. {trap}It is comfortable, and it can replace effort.{/trap} {idea}Ask yourself where the proof is for your own safety.{/idea}
old: Being in the right group guarantees me Paradise.
new: Paradise is not a membership card. I need truth and deeds, not labels.
try: Write one thing you assume makes you safe with Allah. Ask: what is my evidence for it?

title: Submit your whole self to Allah and do good.
subtitle: Sincerity plus doing it right
then: After rejecting the claim, the verse says who is saved: {idea}whoever submits himself to Allah and does good.{/idea} Ibn Kathir: a deed needs two conditions, done for Allah alone and done the way the Messenger ﷺ taught. Such people get {reward}their reward with their Lord, no fear and no grief.{/reward}
now: You pray perfectly, but to be seen at the family gathering. Or you mean well, but invent your own way of worship. {idea}Sincerity and the right method, together.{/idea} Then the worry about tomorrow and regret about yesterday both lift.
old: As long as my heart is in the right place, the form does not matter.
new: A good deed is sincere for Allah and done the way the Prophet ﷺ showed.
try: Pick one act of worship you do daily. Check both: why you do it, and how.

title: Each said the other stands on nothing, both reciting scripture.
subtitle: Dismissing others while holding the Book

picture.label: In front of the Prophet ﷺ

then: Ibn Abbas said a Christian delegation from Najran came to the Prophet ﷺ, and rabbis came to argue with them. {trap}Each side told the other: you follow nothing.{/trap} Both recited scripture. The verse says those without knowledge say the same, and {idea}Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection.{/idea}
now: The comment section under a lecture. One group of Muslims calls another worthless, and they reply in kind. Both quote the Quran. {trap}It feels like defending truth, but often it is ego.{/trap} {idea}Leave the final verdict to Allah, and check your own manners.{/idea}
old: Those people have nothing, I am sure of it.
new: Allah will judge our differences. My job is to be fair and sincere.
try: Before you post a reply in a religious argument online, wait an hour. Then decide if it is needed.

title: None more unjust than one who blocks Allah's name in mosques.
subtitle: Keeping people from remembering Allah
then: Ibn Zayd and Ibn Abbas said this was about the Quraysh leaders who {trap}stopped the Prophet ﷺ from praying at the Kabah{/trap} and turned him back at Al-Hudaybiyyah. The Prophet ﷺ said no one before had ever been barred from the House. Ibn Kathir: {idea}keeping a mosque alive means remembering Allah in it,{/idea} not only decorating it.
now: A newcomer walks into the mosque and gets a stare for her clothes. A teenager is shouted at for his phone and never comes back. A rota fight keeps the doors locked. {trap}We can block people from Allah's house without meaning to.{/trap}
old: Mosques are safe as long as no one attacks them.
new: Turning people away from Allah's house, even by coldness, is a serious wrong.
try: Next time you are at the mosque, greet someone you do not know and make them feel welcome.

title: East and west are Allah's. Wherever you turn, there He is.
subtitle: Comfort for those cut off from their homeland
then: Ibn Kathir says this brought comfort to the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, {trap}driven out of Makkah and away from the Sacred Mosque.{/trap} Ibn Abbas linked it to the change of qiblah, when some asked why the direction changed. {reward}To Allah belong the east and the west.{/reward} Ibn Umar applied it to voluntary prayer while travelling.
now: You moved countries for work. The mosque you grew up in is far away. You pray on a hotel carpet, in an airport corner, in a hospital break room. {reward}Allah is not left behind with the old address.{/reward}
old: I feel far from Allah since I left home.
new: Allah encompasses every place. Wherever I am, I can turn to Him.
try: Wherever you are today, find a quiet corner and pray there with full attention.

title: They claimed He has a son. Glory be to Him.
subtitle: The Owner of all needs no offspring

row.title: a son shares his father's kind

then: Ibn Kathir: everything in the heavens and earth is owned by Allah and is His servant, {idea}so how could one of them be His son?{/idea} He cites the hadith: no one is more patient with hurtful words than Allah; {reward}they attribute a son to Him, yet He still gives them provision and health.{/reward}
now: Think of how quickly you cut someone off for one insult. Then think of Allah, insulted with the worst claim, still feeding and healing the people who say it. {reward}His patience is beyond ours.{/reward} Let it make you humbler with people.
old: I am entitled to cut off anyone who disrespects me.
new: Allah, who owns everything, is patient even with those who wrong Him most.
try: Say subhanallah slowly a few times today, and mean that He is above every flaw.

title: He originated the heavens and earth. He says Be, and it is.
subtitle: Creation without a model, without effort
then: Badi means He created the heavens and earth {idea}when nothing like them existed before.{/idea} Ibn Jarir said Allah also created Isa without a father by the same power. {reward}When He decrees a thing, He only says to it: Be, and it is.{/reward}
now: The debt that feels impossible. The marriage that seems stuck. The illness the doctors shrug at. You have been treating it as too big. {reward}For the One who made the sky from nothing, it is one word.{/reward}
old: This situation is too big to ever change.
new: Nothing is too big for the One who says Be, and it is.
try: Make dua today for the thing you have stopped asking for because it felt impossible.

title: Why does Allah not speak to us? Same words, same hearts.
subtitle: Demanding a private miracle
then: Ibn Abbas said Rafi bin Huraymilah told the Prophet ﷺ: {trap}if you are a messenger, ask Allah to speak to us directly.{/trap} Others said the Arab idolaters said it. Either way, people before them said the same. {idea}Their hearts are alike.{/idea} The signs are already clear for those with certainty.
now: If Allah wants me to pray, He will send me a sign. If this is the right path, something will happen to prove it. Meanwhile the Quran sits on the shelf. {idea}The sign you are waiting for is often the one you are not reading.{/idea}
old: I will commit when Allah gives me a clear sign.
new: The signs are already made plain. Certainty grows by engaging with them.
try: Instead of waiting for a sign today, read one page of the Quran and look for one.

title: Sent with the truth to give good news and warn.
subtitle: The messenger's job, and its limit
then: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ he was sent {reward}with the truth, a bringer of good news and a warner.{/reward} Ibn Kathir: you will not be asked why others rejected you. Abdullah bin Amr said the Torah described him too: {idea}not harsh, not loud in the markets, forgiving and pardoning.{/idea}
now: Your brother stopped praying. Your friend mocks religion. You lie awake as if their choices were your exam. {idea}Your job is to show and tell, kindly.{/idea} The reckoning is Allah's, not yours.
old: If they do not change, I have failed.
new: My part is to convey with kindness. Their hearts are in Allah's hands.
try: Share one good thing about your faith with someone today, gently, then let it go.

title: Their approval has a price. Allah's guidance is the guidance.
subtitle: Chasing approval at the cost of truth
then: Ibn Jarir explained: {trap}they will never be pleased with you until you follow their way,{/trap} so do not chase what pleases them, but hold to what pleases Allah. The Prophet ﷺ was told to say: {idea}the guidance of Allah is the guidance.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says the warning applies to the whole Ummah.
now: You water down your values to fit in at the office party. You drop a prayer so the group is not uncomfortable. You keep adjusting, and they keep wanting more. {idea}Some approval only comes at the price of yourself.{/idea}
old: If I bend a little more, they will finally accept me.
new: I seek Allah's pleasure first. Approval that costs my guidance is not worth it.
try: Next time you feel pressure to hide your faith to fit in, keep one small practice openly.

title: Recite the Book as it deserves: live what it says.
subtitle: What true recitation means
then: Ibn Masud said true recitation is {idea}to allow what it allows, forbid what it forbids, and not twist its meaning.{/idea} Umar said: when they read a verse of mercy they ask for it, and at a verse of punishment they seek refuge. {reward}The Prophet ﷺ himself did this.{/reward}
now: You finish a juz on your commute with earbuds in, racing the next stop. Try one verse instead. When it mentions mercy, whisper: O Allah, give me that. When it warns, say: protect me. {idea}Reciting becomes talking with Him.{/idea}
old: Reading the Quran means getting through as many pages as I can.
new: Reciting it truly means responding to it and living by it.
try: Read five verses today. Pause at each mercy or warning and respond with a short dua.

title: Remember My favour on you. A blessing is a responsibility.
subtitle: Gifts given, then the question of gratitude
then: This call repeats one from the start of the surah. Ibn Kathir says it is repeated to stress following the Prophet ﷺ described in their books. {reward}Allah reminds them of His favours{/reward} and warns them: {trap}do not let envy of what others were given push you to deny the truth.{/trap}
now: You were born into a Muslim family, taught to pray, given a mosque nearby. It is easy to treat that as status. {idea}A blessing is a question: what will you do with it?{/idea}
old: I was given faith, so I am already ahead.
new: Every favour from Allah is a trust that asks for gratitude and action.
try: List three blessings in your faith life that you did not earn. Thank Allah for each one.

title: A Day when no one can stand in for you.
subtitle: Every soul carries its own load
then: Right after reminding them of favours, the verse turns to the Day of Judgement, echoing the warning from earlier in the surah. {trap}No soul will help another, no compensation will be taken, no intercession will benefit, no one will be helped.{/trap} {idea}Favours in this life do not carry over by themselves.{/idea}
now: In the exam hall, your parents cannot sit the paper for you. In the job interview, your cousin's connections stop at the door. {idea}On that Day, it is you and what you did.{/idea} That is sobering, and it is also in your hands today.
old: My family and community will carry me through.
new: On that Day I stand alone with my deeds, so I prepare now.
try: Do one deed today purely for your own account with Allah, not for anyone watching.

title: Ibrahim passed his tests and became a leader for people.
subtitle: Leadership is earned, not inherited
then: Allah tested Ibrahim with commands and {idea}he fulfilled them all.{/idea} Ibn Abbas listed some: leaving his people, arguing with the king, patience in the fire, leaving his homeland, being told to sacrifice his son. Allah made him a leader. He asked: and my offspring? {trap}My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.{/trap}
now: Your father was the imam, so you expect respect. Your family founded the charity, so you expect the chair. {idea}Ibrahim earned his place through tests he passed.{/idea} Your name opens doors; only your conduct keeps you there.
old: My family background gives me a place.
new: Standing with Allah comes from passing my own tests, not from my lineage.
try: Think of the test in front of you right now. Ask Allah to help you fulfil it like Ibrahim.

title: The House: a place to return to, and a place of safety.
subtitle: Purify it for those who worship
then: Allah made the House a place people return to and a place of security. He told Ibrahim and Ismail: {idea}purify My House for those who circle it, stay in it, bow and prostrate.{/idea} Ibn Abbas said: purify it from idols. Mujahid added false witness and sins. {reward}The Prophet ﷺ said mosques are for what they were built for.{/reward}
now: Your local mosque: the shoes piled at the door, the bathroom no one cleans, the loud phone call in the prayer hall. {idea}Keeping Allah's house clean and calm is part of Ibrahim's work.{/idea}
old: Cleaning the mosque is the caretaker's job.
new: Purifying Allah's house for worshippers is a task He gave to prophets.
try: At your next visit to the mosque, tidy something small: shoes, books, a spill.

title: Ibrahim prayed for a safe city with fruits for the believers.
subtitle: Allah's provision is wider than our asking

row.title: if I am provided, Allah is pleased
provision is for all; the end differs

then: Ibrahim prayed: {idea}make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits, those who believe.{/idea} Allah answered that He would also give the disbeliever enjoyment for a little while, {trap}then the Fire.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ said Ibrahim made the House sacred and secure, as he made Madinah sacred.
now: Your salary arrives whether you prayed this week or not. The fridge is full either way. {idea}Provision in this world is not a certificate of Allah's pleasure.{/idea} It is a short loan; what matters is where it leads.
old: Things are going well, so Allah must be pleased with me.
new: Allah provides for everyone here. His pleasure is shown by faith and its end.
try: When you next receive money or good food, say alhamdulillah and ask Allah to make it lead you to Him.

title: Building Allah's House, they still asked: accept it from us.
subtitle: The greatest work, with the humblest prayer
then: Ibrahim and his son Ismail raised the foundations of the House with their own hands. {idea}They were doing one of the greatest deeds ever,{/idea} and their words were not pride but a plea: {reward}Our Lord, accept this from us. You are the Hearing, the Knowing.{/reward}
now: You finished organising the iftar, the fundraiser, the Quran class. People thank you. A small voice says: I did well. {idea}Ibrahim's voice says: Lord, accept it.{/idea} Your big deeds need that prayer most.
old: I did a big good deed, so it surely counts.
new: Even the best deed needs Allah's acceptance, so I ask for it humbly.
try: After your next good deed, say Rabbana taqabbal minna, Our Lord accept from us.

title: Make us submit to You, and our children after us.
subtitle: A prophet still asking to be a Muslim
then: While building the House, Ibrahim and Ismail kept praying. {idea}Make us submit to You, and make our descendants a nation that submits.{/idea} They asked to be shown how to worship and {reward}for their repentance to be accepted{/reward}, though they were prophets doing Allah's work.
now: You worry about your children's faith, scrolling articles at midnight. Ibrahim's way: keep asking Allah for them, and for yourself first. {idea}A prophet asked to be made a Muslim. You can ask too.{/idea}
old: I am already a Muslim, so I do not need to ask for it.
new: Staying submitted to Allah is a gift I ask for daily, for me and my children.
try: Make this dua today for yourself and your family: Our Lord, make us submit to You.

title: Ibrahim prayed for a messenger. The answer was Muhammad ﷺ.
subtitle: A dua answered centuries later
then: Ibrahim asked Allah to {idea}send among them a messenger from themselves{/idea} to recite, teach the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said wisdom is the Sunnah. The Prophet ﷺ said: {reward}I am the dua of my father Ibrahim and the good news of Isa.{/reward}
now: You prayed for years for something and it has not come. Ibrahim never saw his answer in his lifetime. {reward}It came, and it changed the world.{/reward} Your dua for your grandchildren may still be working long after you.
old: If my dua is not answered soon, it is not going to be.
new: Allah answers in His time. Some answers outlive the one who asked.
try: Make one dua today for people who will come after you: your children, students, or community.

title: Who turns from Ibrahim's way, except one who fools himself?
subtitle: Walking away from the clearest path

row.title: Allah alone
sub: never a partner, not for an instant

then: Ibn Kathir: Ibrahim {idea}worshipped Allah alone with sincerity and never committed shirk, even for an instant.{/idea} He disowned every false god, even against his own people. So who would turn from his way? {trap}Only one who wrongs and fools himself.{/trap}
now: You keep a lucky charm in the car. You check your horoscope for fun. You lean on a person as if they control your fate. {trap}Small things that dilute pure trust.{/trap} {idea}Ibrahim's way is simple: Allah alone, all the way through.{/idea}
old: A little of this and that does not hurt my faith.
new: Turning from pure worship of Allah only harms me. Ibrahim's way is the sane one.
try: Find one thing in your life you rely on as if it had power. Let it go today.

title: Submit, said his Lord. I have submitted, said Ibrahim.
subtitle: No delay between the call and the answer

row.title: I have submitted
sub: to the Lord of the worlds

then: Ibn Kathir: Allah commanded Ibrahim to be sincere and submit, and {idea}he complied perfectly.{/idea} The answer is in the past tense, as if already done. {reward}I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.{/reward}
now: The adhan goes off while you are mid-episode. A verse tells you to forgive, and you are still angry. {idea}Ibrahim did not negotiate.{/idea} You do not have to be perfect, just quick to say yes.
old: I will submit once I feel ready.
new: Submission is answering Allah's call now, not when it feels convenient.
try: The next time you hear the adhan today, stop what you are doing within a minute.

title: Allah chose this religion for you. Do not die except as Muslims.
subtitle: The inheritance Ibrahim and Yaqub left their sons
then: Ibrahim advised his sons, and Yaqub did the same: {idea}Allah has chosen this religion for you, so do not die except as Muslims.{/idea} Ibn Kathir: do good all your life and stay on this path, so Allah grants you to die on it, since {reward}a person usually dies on the path he lived on.{/reward}
now: You plan the will, the house, the savings for the kids. What advice will you leave them? {idea}The prophets left one thing: stay with Allah to the end.{/idea} And you cannot choose your last breath, only the breaths before it.
old: I will get serious about religion closer to the end.
new: I die how I live, so I live as a Muslim now.
try: Tell your children or a younger relative one sentence about why your faith matters to you.

title: Dying, Yaqub asked his sons: What will you worship after me?
subtitle: A father's last question
then: When death came to Yaqub, {idea}he asked his children what they would worship after him.{/idea} They said: your God and the God of your fathers Ibrahim, Ismail and Ishaq, one God. Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet ﷺ: {reward}we prophets are brothers with different mothers, but one religion.{/reward}
now: Families gather in the hospital corridor and the talk turns to the house, the shop, who gets what. {idea}Yaqub's last question was different.{/idea} What do your children see you worship: Allah, or work, money and the phone?
old: The most important thing I leave behind is security for my family.
new: The most important thing I leave is my children's worship of Allah.
try: Ask your child or a young relative gently today what Allah means to them, and listen.

title: Their deeds are theirs. Yours are yours.
subtitle: Great ancestors do not cover your account
then: After Yaqub's deathbed scene, the verse closes the story. {idea}That nation has passed. They have what they earned, and you have what you earn.{/idea} Ibn Kathir cites the hadith: {trap}whoever is slowed down by his deeds will not be sped up by his lineage.{/trap}
now: Your grandfather was a hafiz. Your family goes back to a scholar. You mention it at weddings. {idea}His Quran is in his book of deeds, not yours.{/idea} Honour him by doing what he did.
old: My family's piety reflects well on me.
new: My ancestors' deeds are theirs. Only my own deeds speed me forward.
try: Pick one good habit of a righteous elder in your family and start it yourself this week.

title: Join our label to be guided? No: the upright way of Ibrahim.
subtitle: Guidance is not a club membership
then: Ibn Abbas said Abdullah bin Suriya told the Prophet ﷺ: {trap}guidance is only what we follow, so follow us.{/trap} Some Christians said the same. The answer: {idea}the religion of Ibrahim, hanif.{/idea} Abu Qilabah said hanif is what all the messengers believed, first to last.
now: Every group says: come to our circle, our sheikh, our method, and you will be guided. Some of it helps. {idea}But guidance is turning your face to Allah alone,{/idea} not wearing a badge. Ibrahim had no group but the truth.
old: If I join the right group, I am guided.
new: Guidance is the upright way of Ibrahim: Allah alone, whatever group I sit with.
try: Ask yourself honestly: do I follow my circle because it is true, or because it is mine?

title: We believe in all of Allah's prophets and make no distinction.
subtitle: A creed recited before Fajr
then: Allah tells the believers to say they believe in Him and in {idea}everything sent to every prophet, making no distinction between them.{/idea} Ibn Abbas said the Prophet ﷺ often recited this verse in the two rakahs before Fajr. When told stories from the People of the Book, he said: neither believe nor deny them; say we believe in Allah and what was sent to us.
now: Someone at work asks you about Musa or Isa and you realise you know almost nothing about them. {idea}They are your prophets too.{/idea} Believing in them all means getting to know them.
old: The other prophets belong to other religions.
new: Every prophet Allah sent is mine to believe in and learn from.
try: Tomorrow before Fajr, recite this verse in your sunnah prayer, or read a short passage about one earlier prophet.

title: If they believe as you believe, they are guided. Allah suffices.
subtitle: Their choice, your peace
then: The verse follows the creed of all prophets. {reward}If they believe in what you believe, they are guided.{/reward} If they turn away after the proof is shown, {trap}they are only in opposition.{/trap} Ibn Kathir: {idea}Allah will aid the believers and suffice them.{/idea}
now: You have explained your faith to your colleague, your neighbour, your brother in law. Some get it. Some argue, some mock. {idea}You do not have to carry their response.{/idea} Allah is enough for you.
old: If people reject my faith, I am exposed and alone.
new: Allah suffices me. Their acceptance is guidance for them; their rejection does not undo me.
try: When someone dismisses your faith today, say quietly: hasbiyallah, Allah is enough for me.

title: The colour of Allah. Whose colouring could be better?
subtitle: Let faith dye you through
then: Sibghah literally means dye or colouring. Ibn Abbas and many others said it means {idea}the religion of Allah.{/idea} Ibn Kathir links it to 30:30, Allah's fitrah, the natural way He made us on, and says: hold to it. {reward}Who could colour better than Allah?{/reward}
now: Some people wear faith like a jacket: on for Friday, off for the office. Allah's dye goes through the fabric. {idea}It shows in how you drive, how you text, how you split the bill.{/idea}
old: My faith is a part of my life, kept in its place.
new: Allah's religion is a dye meant to colour every part of me.
try: Choose one ordinary part of your day, like driving or shopping, and do it as a Muslim on purpose.

title: Argue with us about Allah? He is our Lord and yours.
subtitle: Ending a dispute with sincerity
then: The Prophet ﷺ was told to cut short the dispute: {idea}do you argue with us about Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord?{/idea} Ibn Kathir links it to 10:41: for me my deeds, for you yours. {reward}And we are sincere to Him.{/reward} Ibrahim was told the same when his people argued with him.
now: The family debate over religion that loops every holiday. The online thread that never ends. {idea}Sometimes the strongest answer is: we each answer to the same Lord, and I am trying to be sincere to Him.{/idea} Then step back.
old: I have to keep arguing until they admit I am right.
new: We each carry our own deeds before one Lord. My task is sincerity, not winning.
try: In your next religious argument, state your view once, kindly, then end it with a sincere wish.

title: Do you know better, or does Allah?
subtitle: Hiding a testimony you hold
then: Some claimed the prophets from Ibrahim to the tribes followed their later labels. {idea}Do you know better, or does Allah?{/idea} Al-Hasan Al-Basri said their own Book stated these prophets were neither, and {trap}they testified to it, yet hid it from people.{/trap}
now: You saw what happened in the car park. You know who said what in the meeting. You were asked, and you said nothing. {trap}Hiding a testimony you hold is called a great wrong.{/trap} {idea}Allah is not unaware.{/idea}
old: Staying silent keeps me out of trouble.
new: Hiding the truth I know, when it is needed, is a serious wrong before Allah.
try: If you are holding back a truth that someone needs to be treated fairly, find a safe way to share it.

title: Said twice: they have their deeds, you have yours.
subtitle: Stop arguing about them; look at yourself

row.title: your deeds
sub: the only ones you answer for

then: The same words that closed Yaqub's story now close the argument over which label the prophets wore. Ibn Kathir: {trap}being their relatives will not suffice{/trap} unless you follow their good deeds. {idea}You will not be asked what they did. You will be asked what you did.{/idea}
now: You can spend hours debating history, which scholar was right, which group owns which prophet. {idea}None of that is on your exam.{/idea} The question is simpler and closer: did you follow them today?
old: Proving who the prophets belonged to matters a lot.
new: I will not be asked about their label, only whether I walked their way.
try: Swap one religious debate you would have today for one act the prophets did: a dua, a kindness, a prayer.

title: East and west both belong to Allah.
subtitle: When people mock you for changing direction
then: In Madinah the Muslims had prayed toward Bayt Al-Maqdis for about sixteen or seventeen months. When the command came to face the Ka'bah, some people said: {trap}what is wrong with them, facing one way and then another?{/trap} The verse answers before the question even spreads: {idea}east and west belong to Allah.{/idea}
now: You start praying again, or stop a habit your friends still enjoy. Someone in the family group chat says, "So now you are religious?" The change looks strange from outside. {idea}You did not switch sides. You followed the One who owns every direction.{/idea}
old: If I change my ways, people will see me as unstable.
new: Changing to follow Allah is not instability. It is the most stable thing I can do.
try: Think of one good change you made that someone questioned. Thank Allah for it quietly tonight.

title: No prayer offered in obedience is ever wasted.
subtitle: A middle community, a test, and a mercy
then: Some Muslims had died before the Qiblah changed, and the believers worried about their prayers toward Jerusalem. {reward}Allah would never make your faith be lost.{/reward} The same verse calls them a just, middle community, and says the change was {trap}heavy except for those Allah guided.{/trap}
now: You prayed for years with little knowledge. Now you learn more and a quiet voice says, "All those years did not count." Or your late grandmother practised as she knew how. {reward}Sincere obedience with what you knew is not erased by learning more.{/reward}
old: Everything I did before I knew better was worthless.
new: Allah keeps what I gave Him sincerely, and the test is whether I follow now.
try: Make a short dua for someone who died before you could teach or learn from them more.

title: Allah saw him looking up at the sky.
subtitle: A silent longing that was answered
then: The Prophet ﷺ prayed toward Bayt Al-Maqdis as commanded, yet he loved the Qiblah of Ibrahim. He would supplicate and keep looking up at the sky, {idea}waiting for Allah's command{/idea} rather than changing it himself. Then came: {reward}We have seen the turning of your face.{/reward}
now: There is a wish you have not told anyone. A job, a child, a healing, a way out. You look up at the ceiling at night more than you admit. {reward}The verse says your silent looking up is seen.{/reward} Keep asking, and keep obeying while you wait.
old: If I do not say it out loud, no one knows what I long for.
new: Allah sees even the turning of my face before I speak.
try: Tonight, look up and name your quiet wish to Allah in one sentence.

title: No sign moves a heart set on its desire.
subtitle: Why more proof does not always help
then: The People of the Scripture knew the truth, yet Ibn Kathir says {trap}no proof would make them abandon their desires.{/trap} Then the warning is aimed at the Prophet ﷺ and his community: following others' wishes {idea}after knowledge has come{/idea} is wrongdoing, because the proof against one who knows is stronger.
now: You know the facts about a habit. The article, the doctor's warning, the ayah. You still scroll past it, waiting for one more proof. {trap}The problem was never missing evidence.{/trap} {idea}Knowing more makes your choice weigh more.{/idea}
old: If I just had more proof, I would change.
new: When desire is in charge, proof is never enough. What I already know is my test.
try: Pick one thing you already know is right and do the first small step today.

title: They knew him like they knew their own sons.
subtitle: Hiding what you clearly recognize
then: The Arabs used knowing your own child as a picture of something {idea}completely obvious.{/idea} Ibn Kathir reports that 'Abdullah bin Salam, a scholar of the Israelites who became Muslim, said he recognized the Prophet ﷺ like that and even more. Yet {trap}a party hid the truth while knowing it.{/trap}
now: At work you know whose idea it really was. In the family you know who was actually wrong in the fight. Staying quiet is easier. {trap}Hiding what you clearly know is its own act.{/trap} {idea}Saying it, gently, is the honest choice.{/idea}
old: If I stay quiet about what I know, I have done nothing wrong.
new: Hiding a truth I recognize as clearly as my own child is a choice I will answer for.
try: Give credit today to someone whose good work you know went unnoticed.

title: The truth is from your Lord. Do not doubt.
subtitle: Steadying the heart after others deny
then: After describing those who mocked the change and those who hid what they knew, Allah {idea}strengthens the resolve of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers.{/idea} What came to him is {reward}the truth without doubt.{/reward}
now: You read a clever post online that makes your faith feel shaky. The comments pile on. Your certainty starts to depend on who sounds louder. {idea}The truth does not get its strength from the comment section.{/idea}
old: If enough people question it, maybe it is not true.
new: Truth is measured by its source, not by how many argue with it.
try: Next time doubt comes from a post, close it and read one ayah slowly instead.

title: Stop arguing about direction. Race to do good.
subtitle: Everyone faces somewhere; all are gathered
then: Ibn 'Abbas said this speaks of the followers of different religions: {idea}each has a direction it faces.{/idea} Allah's answer is not more debate but {reward}hasten toward all that is good.{/reward} Wherever people are scattered, Allah is able to bring them all together.
now: The argument in the comments has run three days. Nobody is changing their mind. Meanwhile the neighbour needs a lift and the charity box is empty. {idea}The verse moves you off the debate floor and onto the race track.{/idea}
old: I have to win this argument first.
new: My time is better spent getting ahead in good than getting ahead in debate.
try: Leave one online argument unanswered and do one good deed in that time instead.

title: Wherever you set out from, face the same House.
subtitle: A command repeated so the heart settles

row.title: Allah sees
sub: not unaware of what you do

row.title: now
sub: it is the truth from Me

then: This is the second time the command is given. Ibn Kathir explains each repetition adds something: first Allah granted what the Prophet ﷺ wished for, and here He states {idea}it is also the truth from Him{/idea} that He loves. It ends with a reminder: {reward}Allah is not unaware of what you do.{/reward}
now: You travel for work, move cities, change jobs. The coffee shop changes, the commute changes, the people around you change. {idea}One thing stays fixed: the direction your heart turns.{/idea} Wherever you set out from, it is the same House.
old: When life moves me around, my faith moves around with it.
new: Wherever I start from, I have one fixed point to turn toward.
try: Next time you are somewhere new, find the Qiblah first and pause facing it for a moment.

title: Fear them not. Fear Me.
subtitle: When critics will talk no matter what
then: The third repetition. Facing the Ka'bah removed the argument that the Muslims were only following another people's Qiblah. Yet {trap}those bent on wrong would still argue.{/trap} So Allah says: do not fear the doubts they raise, {idea}fear Me alone{/idea}, so that I may {reward}complete My favor upon you.{/reward}
now: You change something for Allah and brace for the remarks. Some people will understand. {trap}Some will find a complaint whatever you do.{/trap} Their voices take up your evenings. {idea}You cannot satisfy them. You only have to stand right with Allah.{/idea}
old: I need to answer every critic before I can feel at peace.
new: Some critics will never be satisfied. Fear of Allah is the only fear that settles me.
try: Name one person whose opinion you fear too much. Ask Allah to free your heart from it.

title: A messenger from among you, teaching what you never knew.
subtitle: The biggest favor in the chain of favors

row.title: purifies
sub: from the ills of the soul

then: Just as Allah completed His favor with the Qiblah, He had already given a greater one: {reward}a Messenger ﷺ from among themselves.{/reward} Ibn Kathir says he cleansed them of the worst behavior of Jahiliyyah, when {trap}they used to utter foolish statements{/trap}, and raised them to deep knowledge.
now: Think of the things you know today that you did not know at fifteen. How to pray. How to seek forgiveness. Why kindness to parents matters. {reward}Someone carried that to you, link by link, from him ﷺ.{/reward}
old: What I know about my faith is just what I grew up with.
new: Everything good I know traces back to a gift Allah sent among people like me.
try: Send a short thank you message to someone who first taught you something about Islam.

title: Remember Me and I will remember you.
subtitle: The smallest exchange with the largest return
then: After listing His favors, Allah asks for remembrance and gratitude. Ibn Kathir cites the authentic hadith: {reward}whoever mentions Me to himself, I mention him to Myself; whoever mentions Me in a gathering, I mention him in a better one.{/reward} And {idea}be grateful to Me and do not deny Me.{/idea}
now: You are stuck in traffic, or in the hospital waiting room, phone at 8 percent. You whisper "Alhamdulillah" and nobody hears. {reward}The Lord of everything mentions you in return.{/reward} One small word, a remembrance from Him back.
old: My little dhikr in the car does not really matter.
new: When I remember Allah, even quietly, He remembers me.
try: Pick one daily wait, like the kettle or a red light, and say one dhikr there.

title: Patience and prayer are the two things to lean on.
subtitle: Where to take your strain

picture.label: Every day is one of two

then: Right after commanding gratitude, Allah commands patience and prayer. Ibn Kathir says a servant is always {reward}enjoying a blessing to thank for{/reward} or {trap}facing a hardship to bear patiently.{/trap} He cites the hadith: amazing is the believer, for whatever Allah decrees is good for him.
now: The rent is late, the boss sent a sharp email, the child has a fever again. You reach for your phone to vent. {idea}The verse points to two other tools: hold steady, and stand up to pray.{/idea} Then it adds the part that changes everything: Allah is with the patient.
old: When things go wrong, I have to handle it on my own.
new: Patience and prayer are where I draw strength, and Allah is with me in it.
try: Next time stress spikes, pray two rak'ahs before you message anyone about it.

title: Do not call them dead. They are alive.
subtitle: What we cannot perceive is still real

picture.label: What you see vs what is

then: Placed between commands to be patient, this verse speaks of those killed in the way of Allah. Ibn Kathir says {reward}they are alive and receiving provision{/reward}, and that a hadith speaks of the believer's soul in Paradise too, so naming martyrs is {idea}to honor them.{/idea}
now: Sitting with a family after a funeral, everyone speaks in past tense. The verse does not deny the grief. {idea}It widens the picture beyond what your eyes can reach.{/idea} What you cannot perceive is not the same as what is not there.
old: When someone dies for good, that is the end of their story.
new: Death ends what I can see, not what Allah gives.
try: Make dua today for a believer you lost, speaking of them with hope.

title: You will be tested with something of loss.
subtitle: The test is announced ahead of time
then: Allah tells the believers plainly that tests will come. Ibn Kathir notes the word {idea}something of{/idea}, meaning a little of each: some fear, some hunger, some wealth lost, loved ones dying, farms not giving what was expected. The verse ends with {reward}give good news to the patient.{/reward}
now: The layoff email. The harvest of your hard work smaller than planned. A phone call from the hospital. It feels like the floor gave way. {idea}The verse said it would come, long before it did.{/idea} You are not off the path. You are on the part of it that was announced.
old: If I am losing things, Allah must be displeased with me.
new: Loss was promised as a test, and the patient were promised good news.
try: Write down one loss this year and one thing it taught you.

title: We belong to Allah, and to Him we return.
subtitle: The words that reframe every loss
then: This is how Allah describes the patient. Ibn Kathir says they say it {idea}to comfort themselves{/idea}, knowing they belong to Allah and that nothing is lost with Him. Umm Salamah said these words with a dua when Abu Salamah died, and {reward}Allah gave her better: the Prophet ﷺ.{/reward}
now: The phone screen cracks. The sale falls through. The call comes that your uncle has passed. {idea}Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.{/idea} It is not a phrase only for funerals. It reminds you, in every size of loss, whose it all was.
old: What I lose was mine and it was taken from me.
new: Everything, including me, belongs to Allah and returns to Him.
try: Next small loss, even a dropped cup, say the words and ask Allah for something better.

title: Blessings, mercy, and guidance for the patient.
subtitle: What patience earns
then: After the patient say their words of return, Allah names their reward. {reward}'Umar bin Al-Khattab said: what righteous things, and what great heights.{/reward} He counted blessings and mercy as two good things, and {idea}being guided{/idea} as the heights above them.
now: You held it together at the hospital. You did not lash out after the bad news. Nobody clapped. {reward}The verse says your Lord sent blessings and mercy on you for it{/reward}, and called you guided.
old: Patience just means quietly losing.
new: Patience is met with blessings, mercy, and guidance from my Lord.
try: Remind someone going through a hard time of this verse in one gentle message.

title: Safa and Marwah: a mother's search became a symbol.
subtitle: Old hesitation cleared, and a lesson in need
then: 'A'ishah explained that some of the Ansar, who had once worshipped the idol Manat, {trap}hesitated to walk between Safa and Marwah{/trap} after Islam. The verse says these hills are {idea}among the symbols of Allah.{/idea} Ibn Kathir traces the walk to Hajar, going back and forth in fear and humility until Allah answered her with Zamzam.
now: You are pacing the corridor outside the delivery room, or walking laps around the kitchen at 2 a.m. worrying about money. {idea}Hajar walked like that too, with nothing but her need for Allah.{/idea} {reward}Allah calls even small good done willingly appreciated.{/reward}
old: My anxious pacing and begging are a sign of weak faith.
new: Running to Allah in need is so honored that He made it a symbol.
try: In your next worried moment, turn the pacing into a dua like Hajar's.

title: Hiding clear guidance is a heavy wrong.
subtitle: What happens when knowledge is buried

row.title: one who shares
sub: even fish seek forgiveness for him

then: Abu Al-'Aliyah said these verses came about {trap}People of the Scripture who hid the description of the Prophet ﷺ.{/trap} Ibn Kathir contrasts it: everything asks forgiveness for the one who teaches. Abu Hurayrah said that {idea}if not for this verse, he would not have narrated a hadith.{/idea}
now: You know how to fill out the form your new neighbour is struggling with. You know a short dua that would comfort your friend. You hold it back because it feels awkward. {idea}Knowledge that helps is meant to be passed on.{/idea}
old: What I know is mine to keep or share as I like.
new: Beneficial knowledge given to me is a trust meant for others.
try: Share one useful thing you know with someone who needs it today.

title: The door stays open: repent, repair, reveal.
subtitle: Three steps back from concealment
then: Right after the warning comes the exception. Ibn Kathir says it covers those who {idea}regret, correct their behavior, and explain what they had hidden.{/idea} He adds that even those who once called to innovation or disbelief, {reward}if they repent, Allah will forgive them.{/reward}
now: You told a half-truth at work and the project went the wrong way because of it. Or you kept quiet in a family dispute and someone took the blame. {reward}It is not too late.{/reward} {idea}Admit it, put it right, say what you held back.{/idea}
old: Once I have hidden something this long, I can never undo it.
new: Allah accepts the one who regrets, repairs, and brings the truth out.
try: Correct one small thing you left misleading, even with a short message.

title: The ending decides everything.
subtitle: Disbelief carried all the way to death
then: After opening the door of repentance, Allah describes those who {trap}disbelieve and die while still disbelieving.{/trap} The difference from the previous verse is {idea}the ending.{/idea} Ibn Kathir notes some scholars avoided cursing a specific person {idea}because we do not know how Allah will make his end.{/idea}
now: You look at someone at work or in the family and write them off. Or you write yourself off after a bad year. {idea}No one's story is finished until it is finished.{/idea} The only ending you can work on is your own.
old: I already know how this person will end up.
new: Endings belong to Allah. My job is to keep turning back while I still can.
try: Ask Allah tonight for a good ending, for yourself and for someone you had given up on.

title: No lightening and no delay once it is too late.
subtitle: Why the time to turn is now
then: The verse describes those who died in disbelief: {trap}their punishment will not be lightened nor will they be given time.{/trap} Ibn Kathir ends this passage with a plea: {idea}we seek refuge with Allah from this evil end.{/idea}
now: The reminder on your phone says "start praying regularly." You snooze it again. Next month, after the exams, after the wedding. {idea}Every day you wake up is a reprieve given to you.{/idea} The verse is a warning, but it is also an open window.
old: There will always be time to fix things with Allah later.
new: This life is the time that was given. There is no delay after it.
try: Do today one act of return you have been postponing, however small.

title: One God, and He is Mercy itself.
subtitle: The center that everything else turns around
then: After warnings about concealment and disbelief, Allah states the core: {idea}your God is One God.{/idea} Then He names Himself {reward}the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.{/reward} Ibn Kathir reports a hadith that Allah's Greatest Name is in this verse and in the opening of Al-'Imran.
now: Your life has many pulls: the boss, the bank, the family's expectations, the feed. Each feels like it needs to be obeyed. {idea}There is only One worth that.{/idea} And the first thing He tells you about Himself, after His oneness, is mercy.
old: I have to keep everyone and everything pleased.
new: There is One I answer to, and He describes Himself first by mercy.
try: Recite this verse slowly once today, and name one thing you have treated like a master.

title: Sky, sea, rain, wind: signs for those who think.
subtitle: Proof of oneness in the ordinary
then: Right after declaring He is One, Allah lists the proofs. Ibn Kathir describes each: night and day following each other {idea}without delay for an instant{/idea}, ships carrying goods between lands, rain bringing dead earth to life, winds that bring mercy. {reward}All of it testifies to His oneness.{/reward}
now: Your delivery arrives from another continent. The rain hits the window on your commute. The days are getting shorter. You see it all and notice none of it. {idea}The verse asks you to look again, and think.{/idea}
old: Nature is just the background of my busy life.
new: The ordinary world is full of signs, if I stop and reason.
try: Next time it rains or the sun sets, put the phone down and look for one full minute.

title: Believers love Allah more than anything else.
subtitle: When love is given to rivals
then: Ibn Mas'ud asked the Prophet ﷺ about the greatest sin. He said: {trap}to set up a rival to Allah while He alone created you.{/trap} The believers are different: {reward}they love Allah more{/reward}, revere Him, and depend on Him for every need.
now: Not a statue. Maybe a career, a person, a team, a follower count. The thing you check first in the morning and think about last at night. {idea}Ask what holds the place in your heart that belongs to Allah.{/idea}
old: I love Allah, I just also live for other things.
new: Love for Allah is meant to be stronger than any other love I carry.
try: Notice the first thing you reach for on waking tomorrow. Make it remembrance of Allah instead.

title: The ones you followed will walk away from you.
subtitle: Every tie cut on the Day
then: The verse shows the moment when {trap}those who were followed declare themselves innocent of their followers.{/trap} Ibn Kathir cites Ibrahim telling his people their bond was only for this world, and on the Day {trap}you shall disown each other.{/trap}
now: You follow a person online so closely you take their opinions as your own. Or you go along with your friends because "everyone does it." {idea}Ask: will they stand with me when I answer for it?{/idea}
old: If I am following the crowd or a leader, the blame is on them.
new: Those I follow cannot carry me. I answer for whom I chose to follow.
try: Unfollow or mute one voice that pulls you away from what you know is right.

title: If only we had one more chance.
subtitle: Regret that comes after the door closes
then: The followers who were disowned wish to {trap}return to the world once more{/trap} so they could disown their leaders in turn. Instead, {trap}Allah shows them their deeds as regrets.{/trap} Ibn Kathir notes that if they had known what they would face, they would have left the path they lived by.
now: You are, right now, living the chance those people begged for. The same feed, the same friends, the same choices are in front of you today. {idea}Their wish is your ordinary Tuesday.{/idea}
old: I will change my direction when I am sure it matters.
new: The one more chance others will beg for is the day I am living now.
try: Choose one deed today you would want to see, not regret, on the Day.

title: The earth is spread out for you. Watch the footsteps.
subtitle: Wide permission, and an enemy who walks in steps

row.title: Satan's footsteps
sub: one small step at a time

then: After stating that He alone created everything, Allah reminds people He is also their Provider: {reward}eat from what is lawful and good on the earth.{/reward} Ibn Kathir explains Satan's footsteps as {trap}his ways and methods{/trap}, like the Jahiliyyah custom of forbidding certain camels to honor idols. Qatadah said every act of disobedience is one of his steps.
now: Nobody wakes up and decides to wreck their life. It starts with one late night, one "just this once," one oath sworn in anger. {trap}Footsteps, not leaps.{/trap} Meanwhile {reward}so much good is open to you{/reward} that you barely notice it.
old: Small slips do not really lead anywhere.
new: Satan works in small steps, and Allah has opened far more good than I need.
try: Notice one small step you keep taking toward a habit you dislike. Skip it once today.

title: His worst order: speak about Allah without knowing.
subtitle: Three things Satan commands
then: Ibn Kathir reads the verse as climbing: Satan commands {trap}evil acts, then worse, then what is worse still{/trap}, which is {trap}saying about Allah what you do not know.{/trap} He notes this includes every innovator and disbeliever.
now: Someone in the family group chat forwards a post: "Allah will definitely punish anyone who..." No source, just certainty. You almost forward it too. {idea}Pausing before you speak for Allah is a form of respect.{/idea}
old: Sharing what I think about religion is just my opinion.
new: Speaking about Allah without knowledge is serious. "I do not know" is safer.
try: Before forwarding the next religious message, check its source or let it go.

title: We do what our fathers did. Even if they were wrong?
subtitle: Habit inherited is not the same as guidance
then: When called to what Allah revealed, people answered: {trap}rather, we will follow what we found our fathers doing.{/trap} Ibn 'Abbas said it came about a group who refused the Prophet's ﷺ call this way. The verse asks: {idea}even if their fathers had no understanding or guidance?{/idea}
now: "This is how it has always been done in our family." At weddings, in how daughters are treated, in grudges between relatives. Some of it is beautiful and some of it is not. {idea}The question is not who did it first, but whether Allah approves of it.{/idea}
old: If my family has always done it, it must be fine.
new: I honor my family by keeping what is right and leaving what is not.
try: Name one family custom you follow without thinking. Ask honestly if it pleases Allah.

title: Hearing the call but catching only noise.
subtitle: When words reach the ears but not the heart
then: Ibn Kathir explains the parable: like animals that hear the shepherd but {trap}only catch the sounds, not the meaning.{/trap} Deaf, because they do not hear the truth. Mute, because they do not say it. {trap}Blind, because they do not see its path.{/trap}
now: The Friday talk plays while you check your phone. The Quran recitation runs in the car as background. Your mother's advice comes in one ear. {idea}Sound arrives every day. Meaning only arrives when you lean in.{/idea}
old: I hear plenty of reminders, so I am fine.
new: Hearing the call is not the same as taking it in.
try: Listen to one short reminder today with the phone face down, start to finish.

title: Eat the good things, then say thank you.
subtitle: Food, gratitude, and a dua that rises

row.title: be grateful
sub: if He is whom you worship

then: Allah commands the believers to eat from the good things He provided and {idea}thank Him for it.{/idea} Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of the dusty traveller raising his hands, {trap}'O Lord, O Lord', while his food was unlawful{/trap}, and says pure food is a cause for {reward}supplications being accepted.{/reward}
now: Lunch at your desk, eaten while answering emails. Dinner in front of a screen. You cannot remember tasting it. {idea}The verse pairs eating with thanking, as if the meal is not finished until you say it.{/idea} And where your money comes from reaches your dua.
old: Food is just fuel. What matters is what I do after.
new: What I eat, and how I earned it, and whether I thank Him, are part of my worship.
try: At your next meal, stop for ten seconds and thank Allah for one thing on the plate.

title: Only a few things forbidden, and mercy even in need.
subtitle: A short list, and a door for the desperate
then: After commanding the believers to eat from the good, Allah names {idea}only a short list{/idea} of what He forbade. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith: {reward}what Allah has not mentioned is part of what He has pardoned.{/reward} Even the list ends with mercy for someone driven by real need.
now: A friend says your faith is "just a list of things you cannot do." Look again at the verse. {reward}The field is wide; the fence is short.{/reward} And the One who drew it ends by calling Himself Forgiving and Merciful.
old: Being religious means living mostly with restrictions.
new: Allah opened most things and limited a few, and even then He is merciful.
try: List five good things you enjoyed today that Allah made freely lawful. Thank Him for them.

title: Truth sold for a small price is a terrible trade.
subtitle: Hiding what is right to keep a position
then: Ibn Kathir says those who hid what their Book said did so {trap}to keep the authority, gifts, and honor{/trap} they enjoyed. Yet Allah made the truth known anyway, and the people they feared losing followed it. {trap}Allah will not speak to them nor purify them.{/trap}
now: You keep quiet about a problem at work because speaking up might cost your promotion. You leave out a detail so a sale goes through. {trap}A small price for something priceless.{/trap} {idea}The truth usually comes out anyway. Only the trade remains.{/idea}
old: Bending the truth a little to protect my position is just being smart.
new: Anything I gain by hiding the truth is a small price for a huge loss.
try: Think of one place you stay quiet for gain. Decide what you would say if you were brave.

title: They bought error and paid with guidance.
subtitle: Looking at what you are really paying
then: The verse describes the same people as traders who {trap}purchased error at the price of guidance{/trap} and punishment at the price of forgiveness. It ends with a cry of astonishment at how they could bear what they chose. Ibn Kathir adds: {idea}we seek refuge with Allah from this evil end.{/idea}
now: Every choice has a price tag you do not see at checkout. The extra hour online paid for with fajr. The angry text paid for with a friendship. {idea}Before you buy, read what you are paying with.{/idea}
old: I am not giving anything up, just getting what I want.
new: Every wrong choice is paid for with something good I could have had.
try: Before one tempting choice today, ask: what am I paying for this?

title: The Book came with truth; disputing it pushes people far apart.
subtitle: Why the Book itself is the anchor
then: Ibn Kathir explains the punishment is because Allah's Books {idea}bring truth and expose falsehood{/idea}, and they {idea}ordered people to announce the truth and spread the knowledge.{/idea} Instead, some defied that knowledge, and {trap}those who disputed over the Book ended far away in opposition.{/trap}
now: A study circle turns into a shouting match about who is right. Two cousins stop speaking over an online debate. {trap}The Book becomes a weapon instead of a light.{/trap} {idea}It was sent to guide you, not to win with.{/idea}
old: Arguing hard about religion shows I care.
new: The Book is truth to follow and share, not a stage for disputes that divide.
try: Next time a religious argument heats up, ask what the verse is asking you to do, then stop.

title: Righteousness is not a direction. It is a life.
subtitle: What birr actually looks like

row.title: belief
sub: Allah, Last Day, angels, Book, prophets

then: After all the debate over the Qiblah, Ibn Kathir says this verse makes clear the aim was {idea}obedience to Allah{/idea}, not a direction for its own sake. Then it fills in what righteousness looks like, starting with giving wealth while loving it. The Prophet ﷺ said the best charity is {reward}given while healthy and fearing poverty.{/reward}
now: You arrive early for prayer, perfect row. Then in the car you ignore your brother's call for help with rent, and break a promise to your daughter. {idea}The verse widens the picture: belief, giving, prayer, keeping your word, and steadiness when it hurts.{/idea}
old: If I get the rituals right, I am righteous.
new: Righteousness is faith that shows in my wallet, my promises, and my patience.
try: Give something today you would rather keep, to a relative if you can.

title: Justice for every life, and a door open to forgiveness.
subtitle: Ending double standards, honoring mercy
then: Ibn Kathir explains that before Islam a stronger tribe would {trap}value its own people's lives at double{/trap} and take less for the weaker. The verse ordered justice and an end to such twisting. It also opened room for the victim's family to forgive, which Qatadah called {reward}a mercy not given to any nation before.{/reward}
now: Most of us will never stand in a courtroom over a life. But you know the smaller version: the rules that bend for the boss's nephew, the cousin whose wrongs are always excused. {idea}The verse refuses that.{/idea} And when you have been wronged, it holds open a door: {reward}forgiving, then settling things kindly.{/reward}
old: Some people's wrongs matter less because of who they are.
new: Every life weighs the same before Allah, and forgiving is honored as mercy.
try: Notice one place where you excuse someone close to you but not others. Even it out.

title: In justice there is life.
subtitle: Why fairness protects everyone

key.label: What it feels like vs what it does

then: The verse speaks to {idea}people of understanding.{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains the sanctity of life is preserved because a would-be killer holds back, knowing justice will reach him. He notes the earlier saying that killing stops killing, and that the Quran put it {reward}far more clearly: in it there is life.{/reward}
now: A class where the teacher lets bullying slide. A workplace where theft is ignored. Everyone feels less safe. {idea}When fairness is sure, people hold back from harm.{/idea} Justice is not the opposite of mercy. It is what keeps others alive and safe.
old: Being strict about justice is just being harsh.
new: Fair consequences protect lives and keep people from harming each other.
try: Be fair today in one small decision, even if it is less comfortable than letting it slide.

title: Think of your family before death comes near.
subtitle: Leaving wealth with fairness and care
then: Ibn Kathir explains this verse came before the detailed verses on inheritance, which later gave each heir a fixed share. He cites Ibn 'Umar: after hearing the Prophet ﷺ speak about having a will ready, {idea}no night passed without his will kept with him.{/idea} And a hadith warns that {trap}an unjust will can spoil a lifetime of good.{/trap}
now: Families split over a house, a bank account, a gold set no one wrote down. Siblings stop speaking at the funeral. {idea}A little honest planning, done in health, is a kindness to the people you love.{/idea} Ask a knowledgeable person how to do it rightly.
old: Thinking about what I leave behind can wait until I am old.
new: Caring for my family includes leaving things fair and clear.
try: Write down one thing your family would need to know if you were gone tomorrow.

title: Changing a dead person's words is on the one who changes.
subtitle: The trust of someone who can no longer speak
then: Ibn Kathir includes {trap}adding, deleting, or hiding{/trap} the bequest. Ibn 'Abbas said {reward}the dead person's reward is preserved by Allah{/reward}, while the sin falls on those who changed it. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing: He knows what was said and what was done with it.
now: Your late father told the family who should get his old car. It would be easy to "forget." The paper is in your drawer. {idea}The dead cannot defend their words. Allah heard them.{/idea}
old: No one will know if I quietly change what they wanted.
new: Allah heard what was entrusted, and He sees what I do with it.
try: Keep one promise you made to someone who has passed away, or to someone not present to check.

title: Making peace to fix an unfair wish is a good deed.
subtitle: When correcting is not betraying
then: Ibn Kathir notes a will can carry errors, sometimes {trap}out of the kindness of the heart without thinking of the consequences{/trap}, sometimes by intention. The verse allows someone to {idea}reconcile the parties and set it right{/idea}, so fairness and the deceased's wishes are both respected. That is why it is set apart from the previous verse.
now: Your aunt's wishes leave one sibling out, and everyone is angry. You could pick a side. Or you could sit them down and help them find something fair together. {idea}Being the peacemaker in a family storm is honored.{/idea}
old: Stepping into a family dispute will only make me a target.
new: Helping people reach fairness and peace is a good deed, not interference.
try: If two relatives are at odds, send each a kind word today without taking sides.

title: Fasting was given so you may become mindful.
subtitle: An old practice with one aim
then: Allah addresses the believers and tells them fasting was {idea}prescribed for those before them too.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says fasting purifies and cleanses the soul from bad behavior, and that it {reward}narrows the paths of Shaytan.{/reward} The goal named in the verse is taqwa.
now: Day three of the fast. You are irritable in traffic, snapping at the kids before iftar. The hunger is real, but the verse is pointing past it. {idea}If the fast leaves you a little more careful with your tongue, it is doing its work.{/idea}
old: Fasting is about getting through the day without food.
new: Fasting is training to be mindful of Allah in everything, not only food.
try: Pick one habit, like a sharp word, and "fast" from it today too.

title: A limited number of days, with room for the weak.
subtitle: Built so the heart does not break
then: Ibn Kathir notes fasting was set for a fixed number of days {idea}so it does not become hard on the hearts{/idea} and weaken their resolve. The verse makes room for the sick and the traveller. Ibn 'Abbas spoke of the elderly who struggle to fast, and Anas in old age {reward}fed thirty poor people.{/reward} The detailed rulings are for scholars to explain.
now: Your grandmother insists on fasting though the doctor worries. Your friend on a night shift feels guilty for struggling. {idea}The verse was shaped with weakness in mind.{/idea} Ask someone knowledgeable about your situation, and do not mistake Allah's room for failure.
old: If I cannot do it the hard way, I am failing.
new: Allah built fasting with care for the weak. His room is part of the gift.
try: Check on one elderly or ill person you know during the next fasting days.

title: Allah wants ease for you, not hardship.
subtitle: The month of the Quran, and the spirit of it
then: Allah honored Ramadan by choosing it to send down the Quran, {idea}a guidance for people.{/idea} Even inside the command to fast, the verse says {reward}Allah intends ease for you.{/reward} Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet ﷺ: make things easy and do not make them hard; give good news and do not drive people away.
now: Your cousin is new to praying and you correct every small mistake. Your teenager is struggling with the fast and you lecture instead of help. {reward}The verse sets the tone: ease, not hardship.{/reward} {idea}Make the way to Allah lighter for those around you.{/idea}
old: Faith is supposed to feel heavy, so the harder the better.
new: Allah wants ease for me, and I should carry that ease to others.
try: Help someone with their fast or prayer today in an easy, encouraging way.

title: When they ask about Me: I am near.
subtitle: No middleman between you and your dua
then: Placed in the middle of the fasting verses, Allah answers the question Himself: {reward}I am near.{/reward} When the Companions raised their voices in takbir, he ﷺ told them {idea}you are not calling one who is deaf or absent.{/idea} Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith that the fasting person's dua until he breaks his fast is not rejected.
now: You think you need the right words, the right place, a holy person to ask for you. You whisper in the kitchen while the rice cooks. {reward}He is nearer than you think.{/reward} {idea}Do not grow impatient and say "I asked and nothing happened."{/idea}
old: My dua is too small or my words too plain to be heard.
new: Allah is near and answers, in His way and His time.
try: Make one dua today in your own words, right where you are, before you break your fast or sleep.

title: They are a garment for you, and you for them.
subtitle: A relief, and a picture of marriage
then: Al-Bara' reported that Qays bin Sirmah worked his land while fasting, {trap}fell asleep before he could eat{/trap}, and fainted the next day. This verse brought relief, and the Companions {reward}were very delighted.{/reward} In it, Allah calls spouses {idea}a garment for each other{/idea}, which Ar-Rabi' explained as cover.
now: Your spouse knows your worst moods and keeps them private. You warm each other through long nights with a crying baby. {idea}A garment covers, protects, and stays close.{/idea} When you talk about each other to friends, ask if you are covering or exposing.
old: My spouse is just the person I share responsibilities with.
new: We are each other's covering: closeness, comfort, and protection.
try: Cover one of your spouse's faults today instead of mentioning it, or say one kind thing about them to someone.

title: Winning the case does not make the money yours.
subtitle: A ruling in your favor cannot change the truth
then: Ibn 'Abbas said this is about someone who borrowed without proof, then {trap}denies the loan before the authorities{/trap} while knowing it is not his.
