The Prophet ﷺ said he was only human and might rule for the more persuasive party, but {trap}whoever takes another's right that way takes a piece of fire.{/trap}
now: The deposit your landlord cannot prove you owe back. The client who never put the agreement in writing. A clever argument might win. {idea}Allah already knows whose money it is.{/idea} Qatadah said the dispute will meet you again on the Day.
old: If no one can prove it, it is fair game.
new: A verdict can go my way and still leave me holding what is not mine.
try: Return or settle one thing you owe, even if the other person forgot.

title: Righteousness is not the back door. It is taqwa.
subtitle: New moons, old customs, and the real thing
then: People asked the Prophet ﷺ about the crescent moons, and the answer was practical: {idea}they mark time for people{/idea}, for worship and for Hajj. Al-Bara' said that before Islam people {trap}entered houses from the back{/trap} after assuming ihram, thinking it was piety. The verse says righteousness is taqwa.
now: A cousin swears you must do a special ritual nobody can trace. A post says one odd habit guarantees blessing. {trap}It looks devout.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks a simpler question: are you mindful of Allah? Then use the front door.{/idea}
old: The harder or stranger a practice looks, the more pious it is.
new: Real righteousness is taqwa, not invented outward rituals.
try: Look at the next new moon and use it to plan one act of worship for the month.

title: Even in conflict: do not transgress.
subtitle: Limits that hold when tempers do not
then: Abu Al-'Aliyah said this was the first verse about fighting revealed in Madinah, and the Prophet ﷺ {idea}fought only those who fought him.{/idea} Al-Hasan Al-Basri said transgression includes {trap}harming women, children, the elderly, worshippers in their houses of worship, and needlessly burning trees or killing animals.{/trap}
now: A fight with a sibling, an ex, a coworker. In the heat, you want to use everything: their secrets, their family, their past. {idea}The verse draws a line even in real conflict.{/idea} Do not drag in people who were never part of it, and do not go past what is fair.
old: Once someone wrongs me, I can hit back however I like.
new: Even when I am wronged, Allah's limits still bind me.
try: In your next argument, name one line you will not cross, and keep it.

title: Turning people from Allah is worse than killing.
subtitle: Measuring harm honestly, and respecting the sanctuary
then: The early Muslims had been driven from their homes in Makkah. Ibn Kathir explains that those fighting them were {trap}associating partners with Allah and blocking His path{/trap}, which the scholars called worse than killing. Yet even then, {idea}no fighting at Al-Masjid Al-Haram unless attacked there first.{/idea}
now: Think about the harms you do not count. Mocking someone's prayer until they stop. Making a younger relative ashamed of their faith. {trap}It leaves no bruise.{/trap} {idea}The verse says turning someone away from Allah is among the heaviest harms there is.{/idea}
old: Only physical harm is real harm.
new: Pushing someone away from Allah is a deep harm, even if no one sees it.
try: Encourage, instead of mocking, someone trying to come closer to Allah.

title: If they stop, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
subtitle: The door that stays open even to enemies
then: Right after the hardest verses about fighting comes one short line: {reward}if they cease, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.{/reward} Ibn Kathir notes how at Hudaybiyyah, when news came that 'Uthman had not been killed, {idea}the Prophet ﷺ abandoned the fight and returned to peace.{/idea}
now: Your brother finally stops the silent treatment and sends a message. Part of you wants to make him pay a bit longer. {reward}The verse ends conflict with mercy, not with one more blow.{/reward} When someone stops, let it stop.
old: Once someone has hurt me, I should keep them at a distance forever.
new: When the other side stops, I make room for Allah's forgiveness and mercy.
try: Reply warmly to one person who has tried to end a quarrel with you.

title: No aggression except against the wrongdoers.
subtitle: The aim is an end to oppression, not endless war
then: The verse sets a purpose and an endpoint: until {trap}fitnah{/trap} is gone and worship is for Allah. {idea}If they cease, there is no aggression except against wrongdoers.{/idea} Abu Al-'Aliyah said the Prophet ﷺ fought only those who fought him and avoided non-combatants.
now: A dispute in the family has a clear wrong at its center. Once it is fixed, the anger often keeps spreading: to the in-laws, the kids, anyone on "their side." {idea}The verse narrows it: oppose the wrong, not everyone near it.{/idea}
old: Everyone connected to the person who wronged me is part of the problem.
new: Only wrongdoing is to be opposed, and when it stops, so do I.
try: Be kind today to someone you have treated coldly only because of who they are connected to.

title: Respond only with the like, and fear Allah.
subtitle: Justice measured, not anger unleashed
then: Ibn Kathir says the verse relates to the Prophet ﷺ being turned away from 'Umrah in a sacred month, then entering the next year. Jabir said he {idea}would not fight in the sacred months unless first attacked.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says the verse {idea}ordains justice even with the polytheists{/idea}, and then: {reward}Allah is with those who fear Him.{/reward}
now: Your colleague embarrassed you in a meeting. You plan to embarrass them twice as badly at the next one. {trap}Revenge always wants interest.{/trap} {idea}The verse caps it at the like, then turns your eyes to Allah.{/idea}
old: If someone hurts me, they should get back more than they gave.
new: Justice never goes beyond the wrong, and taqwa often asks for less.
try: Next time you want to get even, do less than the like, or nothing, for Allah.

title: Holding back your money can be your ruin.
subtitle: Spend, do not destroy yourself, and do good

row.title: ihsan
sub: Allah loves the doers of good

then: When people said a fighter was throwing himself to destruction, Abu Ayyub Al-Ansari corrected them: the verse came about the Ansar, who said {trap}let us go back to our estates and attend to them{/trap} once Islam was strong. Ibn 'Abbas said it is about {trap}refraining from spending for Allah.{/trap}
now: Your salary went up. The savings app shows a nice number. The charity request sits unread. {trap}The danger the verse names is not reckless giving; it is comfortable holding.{/trap} {reward}Allah loves those who do good beautifully.{/reward}
old: Keeping my money safe is the careful, responsible thing.
new: Holding back from good can be the real ruin. Giving is safety.
try: Set up one small regular donation today, even a tiny amount.

title: Complete it for Allah, even when the road is blocked.
subtitle: Hajj and 'Umrah, and the day they were stopped

row.title: for Allah
sub: He gave a way to finish

then: Ibn Kathir says part of this verse came in the year of Hudaybiyyah, when {trap}the Prophet ﷺ and 1400 Companions were stopped from reaching the House.{/trap} They hesitated when told to end their ihram, until they saw him ﷺ shave his head, then followed. {idea}Complete it for Allah{/idea}, even when the plan changes. The details are for scholars.
now: You saved for years to go, and the visa was refused. Or you set out to finish the Quran this year and illness stopped you. {idea}The verse is about intention held for Allah and finished in the way He allows.{/idea} When you hesitate, watch how the Prophet ﷺ acted.
old: If I cannot do it the way I planned, the effort was wasted.
new: What I begin for Allah, I finish for Allah, in the way He makes possible.
try: Pick one good thing you started and left unfinished. Do one step toward it today.

title: Pack provisions, but the best provision is taqwa.
subtitle: No foul talk, no sin, no quarrelling on the way
then: The verse sets the months of Hajj and what to leave behind once you enter it: {trap}intimacy, sin, and disputing.{/trap} Ibn Kathir notes some scholars explained fusuq through the hadith that {trap}cursing a Muslim is fusuq.{/trap} Then: {reward}whatever good you do, Allah knows it{/reward}, and the best provision is taqwa.
now: Long queues, heat, crowds, a delayed bus. Hajj or a family road trip, this is where tempers flare. {idea}You packed snacks and chargers. Did you pack patience?{/idea} The verse says the best thing you carry is mindfulness of Allah.
old: As long as I prepared well, the trip will go fine.
new: The most important thing I carry on any journey is taqwa.
try: On your next trip, decide beforehand that you will not argue, and keep it.

title: Earning a living and remembering Allah are not enemies.
subtitle: Trade on the journey, dhikr at the Sacred Place
then: Ibn 'Abbas said people {trap}avoided trading during the Hajj season{/trap}, calling them days of dhikr. The verse said there is no sin in seeking your Lord's bounty. When the Prophet ﷺ left 'Arafat, he told people {idea}calmly, calmly{/idea}, and at Al-Mash'ar Al-Haram he faced the Qiblah and remembered Allah.
now: You feel guilty answering a work call in Ramadan or after Jumu'ah. Or you think your job has nothing to do with your faith. {reward}Honest earning is called bounty from your Lord.{/reward} {idea}The verse just asks you to remember Him in the middle of it, as He guided you.{/idea}
old: My work life and my spiritual life are separate worlds.
new: Honest work is bounty from Allah, and remembering Him belongs in it.
try: Before your next work task, say Bismillah and ask Allah for barakah in it.

title: Move with the people, then ask forgiveness.
subtitle: No special status, and humility after worship
then: 'A'ishah said Quraysh and their allies {trap}stayed in Muzdalifah, considering themselves the people of Allah's town{/trap}, while other Arabs stood at 'Arafat. Islam put everyone in the same place. Then: {reward}ask Allah's forgiveness.{/reward} Ibn Kathir notes the Prophet ﷺ sought forgiveness three times even after finishing a prayer.
now: Your family has a name in the community. You sit in the front row and expect a little extra respect. {idea}The verse puts you in the crowd.{/idea} And after the best thing you did today, the right next step is still: Astaghfirullah.
old: My background earns me a special place.
new: Before Allah I stand with everyone, and after good deeds I still seek forgiveness.
try: Say Astaghfirullah three times after your next prayer.

title: Remember Allah more than you boast about your fathers.
subtitle: When the asking stops at this world
then: Ibn 'Abbas said that before Islam, people at the Hajj gathering would {trap}recite their fathers' deeds{/trap}: he fed people, he paid blood money. The verse turned that energy to {idea}remembering Allah, even more.{/idea} Some would ask only for a rainy, fertile year, {trap}never mentioning the Hereafter.{/trap}
now: Look at your last ten duas. A job, a house, a cure, a good result. All real needs. {trap}How many asked for anything beyond this life?{/trap} {idea}The verse is not against asking for the world. It warns against asking for only that.{/idea}
old: My duas are about what I need right now.
new: I can ask for this world, but not at the cost of forgetting the next.
try: Add one request for the Hereafter to every dua you make today.

title: Good here, good there, and safety from the Fire.
subtitle: The dua the Prophet ﷺ used to make
then: Anas said the Prophet ﷺ used to say this dua. He once visited a man {trap}weak as a sick little bird{/trap}, who had asked Allah to bring his punishment forward into this life. The Prophet ﷺ told him he could not bear it, and taught him this dua instead. {reward}He said it, and he was cured.{/reward}
now: You do not always know what to ask for. The house, or the health? The new job, or the peace of mind? {reward}This short dua covers it all{/reward}, and Al-Qasim said it means a grateful heart, a remembering tongue, and a patient body.
old: I need to list everything precisely or my dua is incomplete.
new: One short dua the Prophet ﷺ loved asks for all the good there is.
try: Memorize Rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanah, and say it in every sujud today.

title: A share for what they earned, and a quick reckoning.
subtitle: Nothing you work for is forgotten
then: A man told Ibn 'Abbas he had {trap}worked for some people and taken part of his wages as a ride to Hajj{/trap}, and asked if that counted. Ibn 'Abbas recited this verse: {reward}you are among those who have a share of what they earned.{/reward} And {idea}Allah is swift in account.{/idea}
now: You went to the masjid on the bus after a double shift. You learned to read Quran in your forties from free videos. {trap}It feels small next to others.{/trap} {reward}The verse says there is a share for what you earned, and Allah keeps the count.{/reward}
old: My modest efforts do not count for much.
new: Whatever I earn of good, however humbly, has its share with Allah.
try: Thank Allah for one good deed you managed this week despite a hard situation.

title: Days of eating, drinking, and remembering Allah.
subtitle: Joy and dhikr together, then the return home

row.title: people return
sub: you will be gathered to Him

then: The Prophet ﷺ called these {reward}days of eating, drinking, and remembering Allah{/reward}, and our festival as people of Islam. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith that Tawaf, Sa'i, and stoning were set {idea}so that Allah is remembered.{/idea} As the crowds head home, the verse says: know you will be gathered to Him.
now: Eid lunch with the family, plates everywhere, kids running. It feels far from worship. {reward}The verse joins them: joy and remembrance in one day.{/reward} {idea}Say a takbir between the second and third helping.{/idea}
old: Celebrating and feasting is a break from religion.
new: Allah made days of joy and food that are also days of remembering Him.
try: At your next family meal, start a short round of Allahu Akbar or Alhamdulillah together.

title: Sweet words, swearing by Allah, and the fiercest in a fight.
subtitle: When the tongue and the heart do not match

picture.label: What you see vs what is

then: Qatadah and others said these verses describe hypocrites in general. Nawf Al-Bikali described people whose {trap}tongues are sweeter than honey but hearts more bitter than aloe.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ said a sign of a hypocrite is that {trap}when he disputes, he goes beyond all bounds.{/trap}
now: You are charming in the meeting, at the family dinner, in your posts. Then the disagreement comes, and you twist facts and go for the throat. {idea}Check yourself in the argument, not in the speech.{/idea}
old: If I speak well and mean well, I am fine.
new: How I fight shows my heart more than how I talk.
try: In your next disagreement, say only what is true, even if it weakens your side.

title: Behind the smile: an effort to spoil the earth.
subtitle: What someone strives for when no one is watching
then: Ibn Kathir notes the verse uses {idea}sa'a, to strive{/idea}, the same word used for hastening to Jumu'ah. Here the effort goes to {trap}mischief, ruining the crops and offspring people live by.{/trap} Mujahid said such corruption can even hold back the rain.
now: Online you post kindness. Offline you spread the rumor that cost a colleague her job. Or you leave litter and waste on land others depend on. {idea}Ask where your real effort goes when the meeting ends.{/idea}
old: What I do when no one is watching is private.
new: Allah sees where my effort goes once I walk away, and He dislikes corruption.
try: Undo one small harm you caused, or clean up one place you left worse.

title: When told to fear Allah, pride drives him deeper.
subtitle: The danger of not taking advice
then: Ibn Kathir says when such a person is told to fear Allah and leave his wrongdoing, {trap}he refuses and becomes angry and outraged{/trap}, because he is used to doing evil. {trap}Pride in the sin takes hold of him.{/trap} The verse ends with a sober warning about where that leads.
now: Your friend says gently, "Maybe don't talk to your mum like that." Your face goes hot. You want to list everything they do wrong. {idea}That flash of pride is exactly the moment the verse describes.{/idea} Breathe, and hear it.
old: When people correct me, they are attacking me.
new: A reminder to fear Allah is a gift, even when it stings my pride.
try: Thank the next person who corrects you, before you reply to the point.

title: Some people sell themselves for Allah's pleasure.
subtitle: The opposite of the smooth talker
then: Ibn 'Abbas said these verses came about hypocrites who {trap}criticized Khubayb and his companions{/trap}, killed at Raji', and this verse praised those companions. Qatadah, Mujahid, and others said it describes believers in general: {reward}those who give themselves seeking Allah's pleasure.{/reward}
now: Not a battlefield. The nurse on a night shift who prays fajr in the break room. The father who turns down a dishonest raise. The student who gives up a weekend to tutor for free. {reward}People spending themselves for Allah's pleasure.{/reward}
old: Giving my time and comfort for Allah is a loss.
new: Spending myself for Allah's pleasure is the best trade, and He is Kind.
try: Give one hour this week purely for Allah's sake, with no one thanking you.

title: Enter Islam completely, not one foot at a time.
subtitle: Wholehearted, not selective

row.title: all of it
sub: as far as I am able

then: Ibn 'Abbas and others said silm here means {idea}Islam{/idea}, and kaffah means {idea}in its entirety.{/idea} Ibn Kathir describes it as holding to all its commands and avoiding its prohibitions {reward}as much as they can{/reward}, and once more, not following Satan's footsteps.
now: You pray but skip honesty in your taxes. You fast but your tongue runs loose in the group chat. {trap}Faith in the parts that fit, absent in the parts that cost.{/trap} {idea}The verse calls you all the way in, as much as you are able.{/idea}
old: I will keep the parts of faith that fit my life.
new: Allah calls me into Islam wholly, step by step, as much as I can.
try: Name one area of your life you have kept outside your faith. Take one step to bring it in.

title: If you slip after clear signs, Allah is Mighty, Wise.
subtitle: Knowing more means standing more firmly
then: Right after the call to enter fully comes a reminder: {trap}if you slip after clear proofs have come{/trap}, know that Allah is Mighty and Wise. Abu Al-'Aliyah and Qatadah said: {idea}Mighty in His vengeance, Wise in His decision.{/idea}
now: You did a course on Islam, read the tafsir, sat with good people. Then the old habits pulled you back. {idea}Knowing better raises the stakes.{/idea} The verse is a warning, but it is also a wake-up while there is still time to turn.
old: Since I know the right thing, slipping now and then is no big deal.
new: The more clearly I know, the more firmly I should hold on.
try: Return today to one good habit you knew was right and let slide.

title: What are they waiting for?
subtitle: Do not delay until the matter is decided

row.title: now
sub: while it is still a choice

then: Ibn Kathir titles this passage {idea}do not delay embracing the faith.{/idea} The verse asks what people are waiting for, if not the Day when Allah comes to judge and {trap}the matter is already decided.{/trap} He cites the verse: on that Day man will remember, {trap}but how will remembering help him then?{/trap}
now: "I will get serious after I graduate." "After the wedding." "When I retire." {trap}You are waiting for a sign that will end the choice instead of helping you make it.{/trap} {idea}The best time to turn is while turning is still yours.{/idea}
old: I will commit fully once I am certain and ready.
new: Waiting for the final sign means waiting until it is too late. Now is the time.
try: Do the one thing you keep saying you will start later, today, even for five minutes.

title: Seeing many signs does not guarantee you keep the gift.
subtitle: Swapping a blessing for its opposite
then: Ibn Kathir lists what the Children of Israel witnessed with Moses: {reward}the parted sea, water from the rock, shade from the clouds, manna and quails{/reward}. Yet many {trap}changed Allah's favor{/trap} by preferring disbelief. The Prophet ﷺ is told to ask them how many signs they were given.
now: The recovery you prayed for. The job that came through. The baby who arrived safe. A year later it is just normal life, and the prayers have gone quiet. {idea}A favor can be exchanged slowly, by forgetting.{/idea}
old: I have seen Allah help me, so my faith is settled.
new: Every sign I was given is a trust, and I can still trade it away if I stop being grateful.
try: Write down one clear answer to a prayer from your past. Thank Allah for it today by name.

title: They laugh now. The final ranking is posted later.
subtitle: When this world is made to look like everything
then: Ibn Kathir describes people {trap}satisfied with this life, collecting wealth but not spending it{/trap} where Allah asked, and mocking believers who give. On the Day of Return the believers are {reward}above them{/reward}, and Allah gives without limit.
now: Your cousin jokes that you are naive for giving to the masjid appeal while he upgrades his car. Your colleagues smirk when you skip the after-work drinks. {idea}The laughter is real, but it is not the last word.{/idea}
old: If people mock my choices, maybe I am the one losing.
new: Mockery today says nothing about who stands higher on the Day.
try: Give something small today that nobody will see or praise.

title: People split not from lack of proof, but from rivalry.
subtitle: Why clear guidance still gets argued away
then: Ibn Abbas said there were ten generations between Adam and Nuh, {idea}all on the religion of truth{/idea}. Then they disputed, and Allah sent prophets. Those given the Book {trap}differed after clear proofs came, out of rivalry{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ prayed at night: guide me to the truth in what they differed over.
now: The family argument that started over one comment and is now about who is right. The online debate where nobody is actually looking for the answer anymore. {trap}Winning has replaced finding.{/trap}
old: When I argue about religion, I am just defending the truth.
new: Sometimes my disagreement is ego, not evidence, and I need to ask Allah to show me the truth.
try: Before your next disagreement, pray the Prophet's ﷺ words: guide me to the truth by Your leave.

title: Even the shaken asked, when is help coming? It is near.
subtitle: The path to Paradise runs through tests
then: Khabbab asked the Prophet ﷺ why he did not pray for their relief. He reminded them how {trap}believers before them endured terrible torture{/trap} without leaving their faith, and said: {idea}you are a hasty people{/idea}. The Companions were later shaken at the battle of the Confederates.
now: Third month of unemployment. The scan results that keep getting delayed. You have prayed, and you whisper, when? {reward}Asking when is not weakness. Even the messengers asked it.{/reward} The reply is: it is near.
old: If I were a real believer, this would not be so hard.
new: Being shaken is part of the path, and Allah's help is closer than it feels.
try: Tell Allah honestly today how tired you are, then say: Your help is near.

title: Your giving starts with the people closest to you.
subtitle: Who comes first when you spend
then: They asked the Prophet ﷺ what to spend, and the answer turned to where: {idea}parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler{/idea}. A hadith in the tafsir lists {idea}your mother, father, sister, brother, then the closest and the next{/idea}. Whatever good you do, Allah knows it.
now: You donate to an appeal online, but you have not called your mother in two weeks, and your brother is quietly struggling with rent. {reward}The groceries you drop at your parents' door count.{/reward}
old: Real charity is giving to big causes far away.
new: Good starts with the people Allah put closest to me, and none of it goes unseen.
try: Do one practical thing for a parent or relative today: a bill, a meal, a lift.

title: You might hate what is good for you, and love what harms.
subtitle: Your feelings are not the full picture
then: This verse came to the early community in Madinah, facing enemies who attacked them. Ibn Kathir notes it was {trap}difficult and heavy on their hearts{/trap}. Then the verse widens: {idea}one might want something that is not good for him{/idea}. Allah knows how things turn out; you do not.
now: The job offer that fell through and broke your heart. The move you resisted that became the best thing for your family. The relationship you begged for that would have hurt you. {idea}You were never seeing the whole map.{/idea}
old: If I hate something this much, it must be bad for me.
new: My dislike is real, but Allah sees the ending and I only see today.
try: Think of one thing you hated at the time that turned out good. Thank Allah for it.

title: A wrong is wrong, but blocking people from Allah is worse.
subtitle: When critics measure only your mistake
then: Abdullah bin Jahsh led a small group to Nakhlah to gather news. On what was {trap}the last day of the sacred month of Rajab{/trap}, a man of Quraysh was killed. The Prophet ﷺ said: I did not command you to fight in the sacred month. Quraysh made it a scandal. The verse {idea}admits the wrong is great, then names a greater one{/idea}: turning people from Allah and driving them out.
now: Your mistake goes viral in the family group chat, posted by the person who has wronged you for years. {idea}You can own your error without accepting that it is the only thing on the scale.{/idea} Then look at your own record the same honest way.
old: Either I admit everything they say or I defend myself completely.
new: I can own my wrong fully and still see the bigger picture fairly.
try: Admit one mistake today plainly, with no but after it.

title: Those who believed, left home, and strove hope for mercy.
subtitle: Even the sincere live on hope, not certainty
then: After Nakhlah, Ibn Kathir reports that the men of the raid {trap}felt they were destroyed{/trap}, criticized by their own brothers. This verse came after: those who believed, emigrated and strove {reward}hope for the mercy of Allah{/reward}, and He is Forgiving, Merciful.
now: You moved cities for a better deen, gave up a well-paid role, kept praying through hard years. Then one bad call and you feel worthless. {reward}Your whole record is still there. Hope is still yours.{/reward}
old: One mistake cancels everything I tried to do for Allah.
new: Sincere effort keeps me in hope of His mercy, even after I slip.
try: Recall one sacrifice you made for Allah, and ask Him for mercy with confidence.

title: Some benefit, bigger harm. And give what you can spare.
subtitle: Weighing honestly instead of just counting gains
then: Umar kept praying: O Allah, give us a clear ruling on wine. Ibn Kathir explains this verse was {idea}the first step{/idea}, before later verses in An-Nisa and Al-Ma'idah. It admits {reward}some benefit{/reward} but says {trap}the harm is greater{/trap}. The same verse asks what to spend: what you can spare.
now: The betting app that paid out once. The scrolling that sometimes teaches you something. You defend it with that one good thing. {idea}The question is not whether there is any benefit, but which side of the scale is heavier.{/idea}
old: As long as something has some good in it, I can keep it.
new: I should weigh the whole cost, not hold on to the small gain.
try: Pick one habit and list its real costs and gains side by side on paper.

title: Care for orphans like brothers. Allah knows who means harm.
subtitle: Handling what belongs to the vulnerable
then: The verse links back: think about {idea}this world and the next{/idea}. Then it answers a question about orphans: {idea}improving their situation is best{/idea}, and if you share life with them, {reward}they are your brothers{/reward}. Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good.
now: You are managing your late uncle's money for his kids. Or you are the auntie raising a niece. You worry about getting it wrong. {idea}Treat them like your own, keep your intentions clean.{/idea} Allah sees the heart behind the spreadsheet.
old: Looking after someone else's child is a burden I just have to manage.
new: They are my brothers and sisters, and Allah knows the good I intend.
try: Check in on a child who has lost a parent, or give something to support one.

title: Choose a partner by faith, not by what dazzles you.
subtitle: What a marriage invites you toward
then: Ibn Kathir notes this verse put {idea}a believing servant above a free, wealthy idolater{/idea}, even an impressive one. He cites the hadith: a woman is chosen for wealth, status, beauty and religion, so {reward}choose the one with religion{/reward}. A spouse shapes where your heart is pulled.
now: The profile with the perfect photos and the great job. The family pushing someone because of their surname. {trap}Impressive can still pull you away from Allah.{/trap} The person you share a home with shapes your prayers, your kids, your Ramadan.
old: If they are attractive and successful, the rest will work itself out.
new: The best partner is the one who pulls me toward Allah, even if they impress me less.
try: Write down the three qualities you most want in a spouse, or value in yours. Is faith on the list?

title: A time of discomfort, not a reason to shut her out.
subtitle: Respect for the body without pushing people away
then: Anas reported some people in Madinah would {trap}not eat with or even mingle with women{/trap} during their period. The Companions asked and this verse came. Aisha described the Prophet ﷺ {idea}resting his head in her lap reciting Qur'an{/idea}, and drinking from the cup where she had drunk.
now: Your sister is curled up with cramps and someone in the house treats her like she is dirty. Or you feel awkward and keep away. {idea}Tenderness is the sunnah here.{/idea} Bring the hot water bottle, sit with her, share the meal.
old: During her period, it is respectful to keep away from her.
new: One boundary is set, but closeness, care, and shared meals stay.
try: Do one caring thing today for a woman in your home who is not feeling well.

title: Even your private life is planting for your meeting with Allah.
subtitle: Intimacy, offspring, and what you send ahead
then: Jabir reported that {trap}a superstition about marriage{/trap} was being spread in Madinah, and this verse answered it. Ibn Abbas explained the field as the place of pregnancy. The verse closes not with permission alone, but with {idea}send good ahead, fear Allah, and know you will meet Him{/idea}.
now: Marriage has its private side, and no one else sees it. {idea}Kindness, patience, and care there are deeds too.{/idea} The children who may come, the way you treat each other behind the closed door, all of it is sent ahead.
old: What happens between spouses has nothing to do with my faith.
new: Even the most private part of my marriage is seen by Allah and can be good I send ahead.
try: Make a short dua today for your spouse or future spouse, and for righteous children.

title: Do not use Allah's name to lock yourself out of doing good.
subtitle: Oaths that block kindness

row.title: keep my word at all costs

then: Ibn Kathir explains the verse as {trap}swearing by Allah to stop doing good{/trap}, like cutting off relatives. He cites the Prophet ﷺ: when I swear to something and see something better, {idea}I do what is better{/idea}. He also cites 24:22, where the generous are told not to swear off helping kin.
now: After the wedding argument you told your brother, wallahi I am done with you. Now he needs help moving and you are stuck behind your own words. {idea}Allah never asked you to use His name as a wall against good.{/idea}
old: I swore it, so now I have to stick to cutting them off.
new: Allah's name is not a tool for my grudges, and choosing the better thing honors Him more.
try: Think of something you swore off in anger. Ask someone with knowledge how to make it right.

title: Allah looks at what your heart meant, not habit words.
subtitle: Slips of the tongue versus intentions
then: Aisha reported the Prophet ﷺ described the unintended oath as {idea}a man at home saying, no by Allah, yes by Allah{/idea}. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said what is held to account is {trap}swearing while knowing you lie{/trap}. Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.
now: You say wallahi ten times a day without thinking. Then once, to get out of trouble at work, you say it knowing it is false. {trap}That one is different.{/trap} Allah is gentle with the habit, serious about the heart.
old: Words are words; swearing is no big deal either way.
new: Allah forgives my careless habits, but what my heart knowingly does is mine to carry.
try: Notice today how often you swear by Allah. Try saying yes or no on its own.

title: Withdrawing from a spouse cannot become an endless punishment.
subtitle: A limit on silent treatment in marriage
then: Ibn Kathir explains the old practice of a husband {trap}swearing off his wife{/trap}, leaving her neither married in practice nor free. The verse sets a limit so that, in his words, {idea}the wife is not harmed{/idea}. If he returns, Allah is {reward}Forgiving and Merciful{/reward} for what was neglected.
now: Days of not speaking. Sleeping on the sofa to make a point. Phone on silent when they call. {trap}Withdrawal can become a weapon.{/trap} The verse puts a fence around it: you do not get to leave someone hanging forever.
old: Going cold on my spouse is a fair way to show how hurt I am.
new: My hurt is real, but leaving someone suspended harms them, and the door back stays open.
try: If you are in a cold patch with someone close, send one warm message today.

title: If you decide to part, Allah hears and knows how.
subtitle: Making the hard decision in full view of Allah

row.title: Hearing, Knowing
sub: He sees how you do it

row.title: once it is over, it is private

then: Ibn Kathir notes from Ibn Umar and many Companions that {idea}a decision has to actually be made{/idea}: return, or part. The verse does not end with a threat but with two names: {idea}All-Hearing, All-Knowing{/idea}. Every word spoken in that decision is heard.
now: The lawyer's office. The family meeting where everyone talks over each other. The messages you send the ex at midnight. {idea}Allah hears all of it.{/idea} Even an ending can be done with dignity.
old: Once a marriage is ending, how I behave does not really matter.
new: Allah hears how I part as much as how I stayed, so I can end things with dignity.
try: If you are in a hard family conflict, reread your last message before sending the next one.

title: Be honest in hard moments. Both spouses have rights.
subtitle: Truthfulness, a pause, and fairness
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah left women {idea}trusted as the authority on what only they know{/idea}, and warned against hiding it. A return is for those who {reward}want to set things right{/reward}. Ibn Abbas said: I groom myself for my wife as I like her to for me, because {idea}they have rights like those upon them{/idea}.
now: You expect your spouse to look after themselves, be patient, keep their word. Do you do the same? {idea}The verse puts both of you under the same standard of fairness.{/idea} Even in a breakup, telling the truth is still worship.
old: In marriage I mostly think about what I am owed.
new: What I expect from my spouse is the measure of what I owe them.
try: Do one thing today for your spouse or a family member that you usually expect from them.

title: Keep her with kindness, or let her go with kindness.
subtitle: No third option of keeping someone to hurt them
then: Ibn Kathir explains that before this verse a man could {trap}divorce and take back his wife endlessly{/trap}. Urwah reported a man telling his wife, I will neither divorce you nor keep you. She went to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse set a limit: {reward}keep her well, or release her with kindness{/reward}. It also tells of Thabit bin Qays's wife, who came to the Prophet ﷺ unable to stay.
now: Breakups get ugly: the gifts demanded back, the threats in the group chat, the custody of the sofa. {idea}Even an ending can be done with ihsan.{/idea} If you stay, stay well. If you go, go with grace.
old: Once a relationship sours, kindness is off the table.
new: Whether I stay or leave, Allah asks me to do it with kindness and stay within His limits.
try: Think of someone you parted ways with. Say one fair thing about them today, or nothing at all.

title: Some words cannot be taken back. Treat them that way.
subtitle: A final line, so the word divorce is never a toy
then: The limit came because the old way was {trap}harmful for the wife{/trap}, as Ibn Kathir says. After the third time, the door between them is shut in a way {idea}no angry man can reopen on a whim{/idea}. These are Allah's limits, made clear for people who know.
now: You say things in a fight you do not mean: I am leaving, we are done, I never loved you. You expect to undo them tomorrow. {idea}Some words do not come back.{/idea} The verse trains the tongue to treat serious words seriously.
old: In a heated moment, I can say anything and fix it later.
new: Some words close doors for good, so I hold them before anger speaks.
try: In your next argument, pause for three breaths before saying anything final.

title: Do not hold on to someone just to hurt them.
subtitle: And do not treat Allah's verses as a joke
then: Ibn Abbas and others said a man would {trap}take his wife back just before her waiting ended, only to stop her marrying again{/trap}, then divorce her and repeat. Some said, I was only joking. The verse says: {idea}do not take Allah's verses in jest{/idea}, and remember His favor.
now: Keeping an ex's things so they have to keep coming back. Refusing to sign the papers to make them suffer. Not answering just to keep them stuck. {trap}Holding on to hurt is still holding on.{/trap} The person most harmed in the end is you.
old: If they hurt me, keeping them stuck is fair payback.
new: Holding someone just to harm them wrongs my own soul more than theirs.
try: Release one thing you are holding over someone: a reply, an item, a signature.

title: Do not block two people who want to come back together.
subtitle: When family pride stands in the way of repair
then: Ma'qil bin Yasar's sister was divorced. When her ex-husband wanted to remarry her and she wanted it too, Ma'qil swore: {trap}by Allah, she will never go back to you{/trap}. Allah knew their need for each other and sent this verse. Ma'qil said, {reward}I hear and obey my Lord{/reward}, and let them remarry.
now: Your sister wants to give her marriage another try and you are still furious at him. Your parents refuse to talk to your brother's wife after a falling out. {idea}Sometimes the obstacle to peace is the family, not the couple.{/idea}
old: After how they treated my family, I have the right to stand in the way.
new: When two people want to mend things fairly, getting out of the way is purer for my heart.
try: If you are blocking someone's reconciliation, have one honest conversation about letting go.

title: No parent should be harmed through their child.
subtitle: Caring for a baby as a shared, fair task
then: Ibn Kathir explains that {trap}neither parent may use the child to harm the other{/trap}: a mother refusing care to hurt the father, or a father taking the child to hurt the mother. Decisions like weaning are made {idea}by mutual consent and consultation{/idea}, which protects the child. No one is burdened beyond capacity.
now: The 2am feed. Arguing over who pays for formula. Or, after a split, withholding visits to punish your ex. {idea}The baby is not a weapon.{/idea} Talk it through, decide together, give what you can.
old: My child is my strongest card in a fight with my partner.
new: A child is a shared trust, never a tool to wound the other parent.
try: Ask your child's other parent, or a parent you know, one question about what they need this week.

title: A widow is given time to grieve, then freedom to live.
subtitle: Mourning with a beginning and an end
then: Zaynab bint Umm Salamah described the old custom: {trap}a widow sat in seclusion for a whole year in her worst clothes{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ said, it is only four months and ten. After the term, {reward}there is no blame for what she does with herself{/reward} in an honorable way.
now: Your aunt lost her husband and the relatives still look sideways when she laughs or gets her hair done years later. {idea}Grief has its season and its dignity.{/idea} After it, she is allowed to live, and even to marry again.
old: A widow who moves on is being disloyal.
new: Allah honors her grief and then gives her back her own life.
try: Call a widow or widower you know. Ask how they are, and listen.

title: Allah knows what you feel. Keep your words honorable.
subtitle: Feelings are not blamed, secret promises are

picture.label: What is allowed, what is not

row.title: a respectful hint
sub: I hope to find a good wife

row.title: a secret promise
sub: promise you will wait for me

then: Ibn Abbas said a man could say in general terms, {reward}I hope Allah gives me a good wife{/reward}, to a woman in her waiting period. What is not allowed is {trap}saying I love you, or making her promise not to marry anyone else{/trap}. Allah knows you will think of them, so He made it easy, and He knows what is in you.
now: You like someone who is going through something hard: a loss, a breakup. You want to message them now. {idea}Your feelings are not a sin.{/idea} But pressuring a grieving person with secret promises is not respect.
old: If I feel something, I should act on it right away.
new: Allah does not blame my feelings, but He asks me to respect someone's grief and timing.
try: If you are tempted to message someone at a vulnerable moment, wait a day and pray first.

title: Even when it ends before it begins, leave a gift.
subtitle: Softening a parting with generosity

picture.label: A marriage that did not start

key.label: What the doers of good do

row.title: ease the hurt with a gift

then: Ibn Kathir says the gift is to {reward}compensate her for her loss{/reward}, each according to his means. He reports that when a marriage of the Prophet ﷺ ended before it began, he {reward}had Abu Usayd give her provisions and two garments{/reward}.
now: An engagement called off. A job offer you withdrew. A business deal you backed out of. {idea}Nothing technically owed, but someone was let down.{/idea} A kind word, a small gift, a thank you softens the blow.
old: If no promise was fully kept, I owe nothing when I walk away.
new: Even a short-lived commitment deserves a generous goodbye.
try: Send a kind message or small gift to someone you recently disappointed.

title: Letting go of what you are owed is closer to taqwa.
subtitle: Do not forget graciousness, even when parting
then: The verse sets a fair share, then opens a better door: {reward}either side may give up their part{/reward}. Ibn Abbas said {idea}the one who forgives is nearer to taqwa{/idea}. Sa'id explained the closing line, do not forget graciousness, as kindness and generosity.
now: Splitting the bill after a fallout. Dividing the furniture, the deposit, the wedding gifts. You could fight for every item. {reward}Or you could let something go.{/reward} Allah sees what you do, especially when no one would blame you for being strict.
old: If I am owed it, I should get every bit of it back.
new: Being fair is good, but letting go of my share brings me closer to Allah.
try: Let go of one small debt or claim someone owes you, and tell them it is forgiven.

title: In the middle of family law, Allah says: guard your prayers.
subtitle: Especially the middle prayer that busy days swallow
then: Ibn Mas'ud asked the Prophet ﷺ the dearest deed to Allah; he said {idea}prayer at its time{/idea}. Most Companions held the middle prayer to be Asr. At the battle of the Confederates the Prophet ﷺ said: {trap}they kept us busy from the middle prayer{/trap}. Standing devoutly meant no ordinary talk inside the prayer.
now: Asr hits at 3:40, right in the meeting, the school run, the custody handover. {trap}That is exactly when it slips.{/trap} The Qur'an drops this verse in the middle of hard family chapters, as if to say: in the middle of everything, keep this.
old: When life is in chaos, prayer can wait until things settle.
new: Prayer is the thing that holds me together while life is in chaos.
try: Set an alarm for Asr today and pray it on time, wherever you are.

title: Even in fear, pray as you can. In safety, remember Him fully.
subtitle: Prayer bends to danger but never disappears

row.title: pray in the form you can

then: After guarding the prayers, Allah addresses a battlefield. Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}pray in the way the situation allows, on foot or riding{/idea}, facing the qiblah or not. Ibn Umar described it this way. When safety returns, {reward}remember Allah as He taught you what you did not know{/reward}.
now: Stuck in an airport, sitting in a hospital waiting room, on a night shift with no break. {idea}Prayer adapts to you; it does not wait for perfect.{/idea} And when you are home and safe again, give it the full care it deserves.
old: If I cannot pray properly, I might as well not pray.
new: Allah made prayer flexible enough to reach me anywhere, so I never have to drop it.
try: Learn one way to pray in a hard situation from someone with knowledge, so you are ready.

title: Do not push a grieving widow out of her home.
subtitle: Thinking ahead for the people you leave behind
then: Ibn Kathir reports that most scholars saw later verses, 2:234 and 4:12, as changing this verse's ruling. Ibn az-Zubayr asked Uthman why he kept it in the mushaf. He said: {idea}I will not move anything of the Qur'an from its place{/idea}. Its spirit stays: {reward}the widow is not to be turned out{/reward}.
now: The funeral is barely over and relatives are already talking about who gets the flat. {trap}The widow feels like a guest in her own home.{/trap} The verse asks: who is thinking about her? Thinking about it before you die is a kindness too.
old: After a death, the property question comes first.
new: The people left behind, especially a grieving spouse, come before the paperwork.
try: Ask yourself who would be left vulnerable if you died, and write one step down to protect them.

title: The God-conscious do not leave someone empty-handed.
subtitle: Provision for the divorced, a duty on the righteous
then: After the verses on widows, Allah returns to the divorced: {reward}for them is a provision according to what is fair{/reward}. It is called {idea}a duty upon the righteous{/idea}. Taqwa is measured here not in ritual, but in how a man treats a woman as she leaves his life.
now: You can be the person with perfect attendance at the masjid and still leave an ex with nothing to start over. {idea}Taqwa is tested at the door on the way out.{/idea} What you hand over then says a lot.
old: Taqwa is about my private worship, not my settlements.
new: How I provide for someone as they leave my life is part of my taqwa.
try: Think of someone who left your life recently. Is there anything fair still owed to them?

title: All these details are made clear so you can think.
subtitle: Rules about real life are invitations to reason
then: This short line closes a long stretch on marriage, divorce, oaths, nursing and widows. Ibn Kathir's tafsir has kept pointing to {idea}the harm each rule prevented{/idea}: the endless divorces, the trapped wives, the year of seclusion. Allah says He makes His verses clear {reward}so that you might use reason{/reward}.
now: You read a long passage of family law and your eyes glaze over. {idea}Behind each line is a real person who was being hurt.{/idea} Slow down and ask: who did this protect?
old: Legal verses are dry and have nothing to say to my heart.
new: These details were made clear for me to understand Allah's care in real-life mess.
try: Pick one verse from this passage and ask yourself: who did it protect?

title: Thousands ran from death. Death met them, then life returned.
subtitle: No caution outruns what Allah decrees
then: Ibn Abbas said these were thousands who {trap}fled a plague, saying let us go to a land free of death{/trap}. Allah said Die, and they died, then He brought them back to life. Ibn Kathir says this shows {idea}no caution averts destiny{/idea}, and is a proof of resurrection. Most people are not grateful.
now: You check symptoms at 3am. You plan every risk out of your life. You are terrified of losing people. {idea}Being careful is good, but it is not a fortress.{/idea} Your safety is in Allah's hands, and so is the life after this one.
old: If I plan carefully enough, I can protect myself from loss.
new: I take care, but life and death belong to Allah, and that frees me from panic.
try: Name one fear that keeps you awake. Hand it to Allah in a short dua before sleep.

title: Hanging back does not add a single day to your life.
subtitle: Allah hears and knows those who stand up
then: Right after the story of those who fled, the community in Madinah is told to stand firm in Allah's cause. Ibn Kathir: {idea}abandoning it will neither bring the appointed term closer nor delay it{/idea}. Khalid bin al-Walid, after countless battles, {trap}died in his bed{/trap}, sad he had not died a martyr.
now: You avoid speaking up for a colleague because it might cost you. You skip the hard but right thing because it feels risky. {idea}Fear tells you hiding buys safety.{/idea} Allah hears the word you did not say.
old: Staying out of the hard things keeps me safe.
new: My time is already written, so I can stand up for what is right without that fear.
try: Do one brave right thing today you have been avoiding out of fear.

title: Lend to Allah. He multiplies it, and He controls the supply.
subtitle: Giving as a loan to the One who never defaults
then: Ibn Kathir notes that in the hadith of Allah descending in the last third of the night, He asks: {idea}who will lend to One who is neither poor nor unjust?{/idea} He links this verse to the {reward}seed that grows seven ears{/reward}. Allah is the one who withholds and grants, and to Him you return.
now: Payday. Rent out, bills out, and a fundraiser link in the family group chat. {trap}Your gut says you cannot afford it.{/trap} The verse reframes: this is a loan to Allah, and He decides what fills your account next month.
old: Every pound I give away is gone.
new: What I give for Allah is a loan He will repay many times over.
try: Give a small amount today and say to yourself: this is a loan to Allah.

title: They begged for the chance, then walked away when it came.
subtitle: Big promises made before the test arrives
then: Mujahid said the prophet here was Samuel. Wahb says the Children of Israel had {trap}lost their land, their children, and the Ark{/trap}. They demanded a king to lead them. Their prophet asked: would you hold back if it were prescribed? They swore not. When it came, {trap}most turned away{/trap}.
now: If I just had the time, I would memorize Qur'an. If I just had the money, I would give. Then the free weekend comes, the bonus arrives. {trap}The promise evaporates.{/trap} Allah knows the gap between what we say and what we do.
old: If the right situation came, I would definitely step up.
new: The test is not what I promise beforehand, but what I do when the moment arrives.
try: Pick one thing you keep saying you would do if only. Do a small part of it today.

title: Allah chose the poor water-carrier. Knowledge and strength over status.
subtitle: When we judge who deserves to lead
then: Ibn Kathir says Talut was {trap}not from the royal house of Judah, and was poor{/trap}; some said he carried water, others that he dyed leather. The people argued with their prophet instead of accepting. He replied: {reward}Allah chose him and increased him in knowledge and stature{/reward}. Allah gives authority to whom He wills.
now: The new manager came from the warehouse floor, not the right university. The imam is young and from the wrong family. {trap}You catch yourself sneering.{/trap} The verse asks: is your objection about ability, or about pride?
old: Leaders should come from the right background and the right money.
new: Allah raises people by knowledge and strength, and my pride is no judge of who deserves it.
try: Say one sincere word of support to someone in a role you secretly thought you deserved more.

title: The sign came with sakinah: calm sent down from your Lord.
subtitle: What returned to them with the Ark
then: Their prophet promised the {reward}Ark taken by their enemy would come back{/reward}. Qatadah and Ar-Rabi said the sakinah in it meant grace and mercy. Ibn Abbas said it held {reward}Moses' staff and remnants of the Tablets{/reward}, and that angels carried it until they placed it before Talut while people watched.
now: Before the job interview, the surgery, the hard conversation, you want a guarantee. What you need first is a settled heart. {reward}Sakinah is the gift that comes before victory.{/reward} Ask for it by name.
old: I will feel calm once everything works out.
new: Calm is something Allah sends down, and I can ask Him for it before anything works out.
try: Before your next stressful moment, ask Allah: send down sakinah on my heart.

title: A handful from the river, or drink your fill and fall away.
subtitle: Small restraints sort out who is ready
then: Talut's army met a river. Ibn Abbas said: {reward}whoever took a handful was quenched; whoever drank freely stayed thirsty{/reward}. Al-Bara said the Companions at Badr were about the same number as those who crossed with Talut, a little over three hundred. Facing Goliath, the certain ones said: {idea}how often has a small group overcome a large one{/idea}.
now: The snack drawer. The extra hour of scrolling. One more episode. {trap}Drinking your fill never quite satisfies.{/trap} A handful is enough, and the small restraints build the person who can face the big tests.
old: Small indulgences do not matter when the big test comes.
new: The way I handle a small thirst trains me for the big battle.
try: Pick one craving today and stop at a handful.

title: Pour patience on us, plant our feet, give us victory.
subtitle: The dua of the few before the giant
then: When the few under Talut faced the many under Goliath, they did not boast. Ibn Kathir says they asked Allah to {reward}send down patience from Him{/reward}, to {reward}keep their feet firm and save them from running away and feebleness{/reward}, and to grant victory.
now: The exam hall. The courtroom. Facing a boss twice your size in the company. {idea}You do not have to manufacture courage.{/idea} You can ask for it to be poured on you like water.
old: I have to find the strength in myself to face this.
new: Patience and steady feet are gifts I can ask Allah to pour on me.
try: Memorize this dua today: Rabbana afrigh alayna sabran wa thabbit aqdamana.

title: A young soldier, David, felled the giant by Allah's permission.
subtitle: How Allah keeps the earth from ruin

row.title: the strong do as they like

then: Ibn Kathir notes Israelite reports that {idea}David killed Goliath with a sling{/idea}. Allah then gave him kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed. If Allah did not {idea}push back some people by means of others{/idea}, the earth would be corrupted; Ibn Kathir links this to 22:40, where houses of worship would be torn down.
now: The bully in the office who no one stands up to. The neighbor who intimidates the street. {idea}Allah often stops harm through ordinary people who step in.{/idea} Sometimes that person is you.
old: Someone else will deal with the injustice around me.
new: Allah protects the earth through people who stand up, and I might be one of them.
try: Step in kindly for one person being treated unfairly today, even in a small way.

title: These stories are told to you in truth. You are a messenger.
subtitle: Why old stories land on the Prophet ﷺ
then: Ibn Kathir says these verses tell the story {idea}exactly as it happened{/idea}, matching what remained in the earlier scriptures. Then Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ directly: {reward}you are one of the messengers{/reward}. The small band in Madinah heard their own situation in the few who crossed the river.
now: You read about Talut and think it is a children's story. But you are the one facing a giant at work, at home, in your own habits. {idea}It is told to you in truth, for you.{/idea}
old: Quran stories are history lessons about other people.
new: These stories are true and told to me, for the giants I face today.
try: Retell the Talut story to a child or friend tonight in your own words.

title: Allah ranked the messengers. Do not turn them into a fight.
subtitle: Honor all the prophets without point-scoring
then: Ibn Kathir reports a Muslim who {trap}slapped a Jewish man in an argument over Moses' rank{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ said: {idea}do not prefer me over the prophets{/idea}, and spoke of seeing Moses holding the Throne on the Day. Ranking belongs to Allah, not to our quarrels. Later generations still fought after clear proofs, by Allah's will.
now: The comment thread where someone insults another faith's prophet, and you want to hit back harder. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ himself told us not to turn the prophets into a contest.{/idea} Respect them all, and let Allah rank them.
old: Defending my faith means proving my prophet is the best in every argument.
new: I honor every messenger Allah sent, and leave their ranking to Him.
try: Read about one prophet you know little about today, with respect.

title: Spend now. A Day is coming with no deals and no connections.
subtitle: The window to give closes

picture.label: What will not work on that Day

then: Ibn Kathir says Allah tells believers to {reward}rush to spend in this life{/reward}, before a Day when no one can {trap}ransom himself even with the earth's fill of gold{/trap}, and friendship and relations will not help. He links it to 23:101: no kinship that Day.
now: You know a guy who can get you in anywhere. Your cousin sorts every problem. Your card has a high limit. {trap}None of that works on that Day.{/trap} What you gave from it today does.
old: I will give generously once I have more saved up.
new: Today is the only time giving still counts; on that Day nothing can be bought.
try: Give something today from this month's money, not from some future surplus.

title: The Ever-Living who never sleeps holds everything, without tiring.
subtitle: Ayat al-Kursi, the greatest verse
then: The Prophet ﷺ asked Ubayy bin Ka'b which verse was greatest. He said Ayat al-Kursi, and the Prophet ﷺ said: {reward}congratulations on your knowledge{/reward}. In Abu Hurayrah's story, even Shaytan admitted that reciting it at bedtime brings {idea}a guard from Allah until morning{/idea}. The Prophet ﷺ said: he told the truth, though he is a liar.
now: Lying in bed replaying the bills, the kids, the scan results. You feel like you have to stay awake to hold it together. {idea}You do not.{/idea} The One who holds the heavens and earth does not get tired, and He does not sleep.
old: If I stop worrying, everything will fall apart.
new: The One who never sleeps is holding everything, so I can rest.
try: Recite Ayat al-Kursi tonight before sleeping, slowly, thinking about each line.

title: Faith cannot be forced. Hold the handhold that never breaks.
subtitle: Truth is clear enough to stand without pressure
then: Ibn Kathir: {idea}do not force anyone into Islam, for its proofs are plain and clear{/idea}. Ibn Abbas said the verse came about Ansar children raised among a Jewish tribe; when that tribe left, the parents wanted to keep them. Abdullah bin Salam dreamed of {reward}climbing a pillar and grasping a handle{/reward}; the Prophet ﷺ said: that is the firmest handhold.
now: You want your teenager to pray, your friend to come back to faith. You nag, guilt, push. {idea}Faith cannot be installed from outside.{/idea} Show it clearly, live it well, and let them reach for the handle themselves.
old: If I push hard enough, I can make someone believe.
new: Truth is clear enough on its own; my job is to show it, and hold tight myself.
try: Replace one nagging reminder to someone with a kind example of what you hope for them.

title: Allah brings you from many darknesses into one light.
subtitle: Truth is one, falsehood comes in many forms
then: Ibn Kathir notes that {idea}light is singular and darkness plural{/idea}, because truth is one while falsehood has many branches. He cites 6:153: follow My straight path, {trap}not other paths that scatter you{/trap}. Allah takes believers out of the darkness of doubt and hesitation.
now: Doubt at 2am. Anxiety about the future. Envy watching other people's lives online. {trap}Each darkness feels different.{/trap} The way out is the same one light, and Allah is the one who leads you there.
old: I have too many problems to know where to start.
new: My darknesses are many, but the way out is one, and Allah is my guide to it.
try: Name one darkness you are in right now and ask Allah, as your Wali, to bring you out.

title: Power made him argue with God. The sunrise left him speechless.
subtitle: When authority goes to your head

row.title: bring the sun from the west

then: Mujahid said the king was Nimrod. Ibn Kathir says {trap}his long rule made him tyrannical{/trap} until he claimed to give life and death himself. Ibrahim answered with the sun: {idea}Allah brings it from the east, so bring it from the west{/idea}. The king was left with nothing to say.
now: The promotion that makes you short with the junior staff. The admin rights in the group chat. Being the eldest who always decides. {trap}A little power makes it easy to forget who gave it.{/trap}
old: Because I am in charge, my view is the one that counts.
new: Any authority I have is on loan from the One who moves the sun.
try: Watch the sunrise or sunset today and remember who controls it.

title: He doubted the ruin could live. He woke a century later.
subtitle: Allah shows you, slowly, that He can restore
then: Ali and Ibn Abbas said this was Uzayr. He passed a ruined town and wondered {trap}how Allah could ever revive it{/trap}. Allah let him die for a century; he woke thinking it was part of a day. His figs and juice had not spoiled, and he watched {reward}his donkey's bones gathered and covered in flesh{/reward}.
now: Your marriage feels like a ruin. Your faith feels empty. Your hometown or your health has collapsed. {trap}You stand there thinking, how could this ever come back?{/trap} Allah restores things that look fully dead.
old: Some things are too broken to ever be restored.
new: If Allah can raise a hundred-year-old ruin, He can restore what I think is lost.
try: Make dua today for one thing in your life you had given up as too broken.

title: Ibrahim believed, and still asked to see so his heart could rest.
subtitle: Wanting certainty is not the same as doubt
then: The Prophet ﷺ said: {idea}we are more liable to seek certainty than Ibrahim{/idea}. Allah had him call four birds back from the hills, and they came rushing. Ibn Abbas called this {reward}the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an{/reward}, because Allah accepted Ibrahim's simple yes, and it speaks to the doubts Shaytan whispers into hearts.
now: You pray, you fast, you believe. And sometimes a question still gnaws at you at night. {reward}That does not make you a hypocrite.{/reward} Even Ibrahim asked to see. Bring the question to Allah, not away from Him.
old: If I have questions about my faith, I must not really believe.
new: I can believe and still ask Allah to settle my heart, as Ibrahim did.
try: Take one question you have been afraid to ask about faith and ask someone you trust.

title: You give one. Allah grows it to seven hundred.
subtitle: How spending for Allah is counted
