row.title: times 700
sub: planted, not spent, and more for whom He wills

then: New community in Madinah, poor, building a mosque, feeding migrants. Giving felt like losing. {idea}Allah showed them farming instead of subtracting.{/idea}
now: Salary just hit. Rent, bills, a bit left. The donation link is open. Your brain says {trap}"minus 50."{/trap} The verse says {reward}"times 700."{/reward}
old: Giving is subtraction from my account.
new: Giving is planting. The seed leaves my hand so it can grow.
try: Give one small amount today. Picture seven ears.

title: Give, then never bring it up again.
subtitle: The gift that is not followed by reminders

row.title: the moment I hand it over

then: Ibn Kathir: Allah praises those who give and then {trap}do not remind the receiver, by word or action{/trap}, nor harm them. Their reward is {reward}with their Lord Himself{/reward}, with no fear on the Day and no grief over what they leave behind.
now: You lent your brother money last year. Every family dinner, you drop a little hint. You paid for your friend's ticket and mention it when you argue. {trap}Each hint takes a bite out of the gift.{/trap}
old: I gave it, so I have a right to mention it now and then.
new: A gift is complete when I let it go and never use it against anyone.
try: Think of something you gave that you keep bringing up. Decide today never to mention it again.

title: A kind word and forgiveness beat charity that stings.
subtitle: When you cannot give without hurting, give words instead
then: Ibn Kathir explains the kind word as {reward}compassionate speech and a dua for Muslims{/reward}, and forgiveness as {reward}pardoning a wrong done to you{/reward}. These are better than charity followed by injury. Allah is Rich, needing nothing, and Forbearing.
now: Someone asks you for help on a day you are broke and irritated. You could throw a fiver at them with a lecture. {reward}Or you could say, I cannot today, may Allah make it easy for you, and mean it.{/reward}
old: Giving something is always better than giving nothing.
new: A gentle word or a pardon can be worth more than money given with a sting.
try: The next time you have to say no to someone asking, say it with a sincere dua for them.

title: Charity for show is dust on a rock. Rain leaves it bare.
subtitle: How reminders and showing off erase a deed

key.label: What it looked like vs what it was

then: Ibn Kathir describes the show-off who {trap}pretends to give for Allah but seeks people's praise{/trap}. His deeds are like dust on a smooth rock: they look plentiful, then {trap}a downpour leaves it bare{/trap}. Ad-Dahhak said the parable also fits the one who gives and then reminds or harms.
now: The donation screenshot posted to your story. The fundraiser where you make sure your name is read out. {trap}It looks like a lot of dust on the rock.{/trap} Ask yourself who the gift was really for.
old: As long as the money reaches the needy, my motive does not matter.
new: If I give to be seen, the rain can wash away everything I thought I had.
try: Give one gift this week that nobody, not even your closest friend, will know about.

title: Sincere giving is a hilltop garden. Even a drizzle makes it fruit.
subtitle: The opposite of dust on a rock
then: Right after the bare rock comes the garden. Those who give {idea}seeking only Allah's pleasure, certain He will reward them{/idea}, are like a garden on a height. Ibn Kathir says {reward}if heavy rain does not fall, light rain suffices{/reward}: the believer's good deeds never become barren.
now: You only have a little to give this month, a coin in the box, a sandwich for the man at the station. {reward}With sincerity, that drizzle is enough.{/reward} Allah sees what you do.
old: My small gifts are too little to matter.
new: Given sincerely, even a small gift falls on fertile ground and grows.
try: Give something small today and quietly say: for You, Allah.

title: A lifetime garden burned just when he was old and needed it.
subtitle: Do not undo your good deeds at the end
then: Umar asked the Companions who this verse was about; they said Allah knows best. Young Ibn Abbas spoke up: {idea}it is a parable for a deed{/idea}, a man who did good, then {trap}turned to disobedience until he annulled his good works{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ used to pray: make Your widest provision for me in my old age.
now: Years of volunteering, then a bitter falling-out that turns into slander. A lifetime of prayer, then a business deal that cheats people. {trap}A good garden can burn late.{/trap} Protect what you built.
old: I have done enough good in my life; I am set.
new: My good deeds are a garden I must keep guarding until my last day.
try: Make the Prophet's ﷺ dua today: O Allah, make Your widest provision for me in my old age.

title: Do not give Allah what you would only take with eyes closed.
subtitle: Giving from the best, not the leftovers
then: Al-Bara said the Ansar would {reward}hang date branches in the Prophet's masjid ﷺ for the poor emigrants{/reward}. Some {trap}slipped in poor dates among the good{/trap}. Ibn Abbas said: how do you accept for Me what you would not accept for yourselves? Allah is Rich and Praiseworthy.
now: Clearing out your wardrobe and sending the stained shirts to the charity bag. Donating the expired tins from the back of the cupboard. {idea}Would you take it with your eyes open?{/idea}
old: Charity is a good place for the things I do not need anymore.
new: I give Allah the kind of thing I would be happy to receive myself.
try: Give away one thing in good condition that you actually like.

title: Shaytan whispers you will go broke. Allah promises forgiveness and more.
subtitle: Two voices when you reach for your wallet
then: The Prophet ﷺ said Shaytan and the angel both touch the heart. {trap}Shaytan's touch threatens evil and denies truth{/trap}; {reward}the angel's touch promises good and confirms truth{/reward}. Whoever feels the first should seek refuge in Allah. Then he recited this verse.
now: You see the appeal for the flood victims. A voice says: rent is due, you cannot afford this, be sensible. {trap}Notice where that voice comes from.{/trap} Allah's promise is forgiveness and more, not less.
old: My fear of running out is just being responsible.
new: The fear of poverty that stops all giving is a whisper, and Allah promises more.
try: Next time fear stops you from giving, say a'udhu billah and give a little anyway.

title: Whoever is given wisdom has been given a lot of good.
subtitle: The gift worth envying
then: Ibn Abbas said wisdom here is {idea}knowledge of the Qur'an{/idea}: its clear and less clear parts, what it permits and forbids, its parables. Ibn Mas'ud heard the Prophet ﷺ say {reward}no envy except in two{/reward}: a man given wealth who spends it rightly, and a man given wisdom who judges by it and teaches it.
now: You scroll past the influencer's holiday and feel a pang. {idea}The person truly worth envying is the one who understands the Qur'an and lives it.{/idea} That gift is still on offer to you.
old: The people I admire most are the ones with the best lifestyle.
new: Wisdom from Allah is the real wealth, and I can ask Him for it.
try: Spend ten minutes today reading the explanation of one verse you recite often.

title: Every coin you spend and every vow you make, Allah knows.
subtitle: Nothing given is lost or unseen
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah has {idea}perfect knowledge of every good deed, charity and vow{/idea}, and rewards greatly when it is done for His Face. Those who turn away from Him have {trap}no helpers{/trap} to save them on the Day.
now: The vow you made in the hospital corridor: if she pulls through, I will. The monthly direct debit no one knows about. {idea}Allah knows every one.{/idea} Have you kept the promise you made when you were scared?
old: Promises made in a crisis do not really count once it passes.
new: Allah knows every promise I made Him and every coin I gave.
try: Remember one promise you made to Allah in a hard moment. Take one step to keep it.

title: Giving openly is good. Giving secretly to the poor is better.
subtitle: So hidden your left hand does not know
then: Ibn Kathir says concealing charity is better because {idea}it protects you from showing off{/idea}, though open giving is better when others will copy it. Among the seven shaded on the Day is {reward}one who gives so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right gave{/reward}.
now: The bank transfer with no reference name. The envelope slipped under a neighbor's door. The bill quietly paid at the counter for the family behind you. {reward}No one claps.{/reward} That is the point.
old: If no one knows I gave, it does not inspire anyone.
new: Open giving has its place, but my secret gifts protect my heart and reach Allah directly.
try: Give one anonymous gift today.

title: Guiding them is not your job. Your giving is for you.
subtitle: Kindness to those who do not share your faith
then: Ibn Abbas said the Companions {trap}disliked giving charity to their polytheist relatives{/trap}, until this verse came. Ata said you will not be asked about the receiver. The Prophet ﷺ told of a man who unknowingly gave to a thief, a rich man, and an adulteress; he was told {reward}your charity was accepted{/reward}, perhaps it would change them.
now: Your uncle who mocks your faith is struggling with rent. The neighbor of another religion just lost her job. {idea}You are not their judge, and you do not control their hearts.{/idea} Help them for Allah's sake.
old: My charity should only go to people who deserve it.
new: Guidance belongs to Allah; my job is to give sincerely, and the reward is mine.
try: Do one kind, practical thing for a relative or neighbor you disagree with.

title: The neediest are often the ones too dignified to ask.
subtitle: Look for the poor who look fine
then: These were {idea}emigrants in Madinah who had left everything{/idea} and could not travel to earn. The ignorant {trap}thought them rich because of their restraint{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ said the truly needy is not the one turned away by a date or two, but {idea}the one who has not enough, whom no one notices, and who asks no one{/idea}.
now: The colleague who always says she is fine but brings no lunch. The student who never joins the group meals. The single dad who keeps quiet. {idea}Look again.{/idea} Find a way to give that does not cost them their dignity.
old: If someone needed help, they would ask for it.
new: The people most in need are often silent, and I should look for them.
try: Think of one person who might be quietly struggling. Find a gentle way to help.

title: Night and day, secret and open: giving as a way of life.
subtitle: Generosity in every season
then: This verse closes the long passage on charity with a portrait: people who give {reward}by night and by day, secretly and publicly{/reward}. Not one big donation, but a life. Their reward is with their Lord, and {idea}no fear or grief{/idea} touches them.
now: You give generously in the last ten nights of Ramadan, then the rest of the year it stops. {idea}What if giving were part of your Tuesday?{/idea} A small regular amount, at any hour, in any mood.
old: Charity is something I do at special times.
new: Giving can be the rhythm of my ordinary days and nights.
try: Set up a small, regular donation today, even a tiny one.

title: They said trade and riba are the same. Allah drew the line.
subtitle: Profiting from another's need versus fair exchange
then: This passage follows the verses on charity, as Ibn Kathir notes: {reward}the givers{/reward} are followed by {trap}those who take people's money unjustly{/trap}. The argument, trade is just like riba, is answered: Allah permitted one and forbade the other. He knows what harms His servants and is {idea}more merciful to them than a mother to her infant{/idea}. Whoever stops, the past is with Allah.
now: Being sure every deal is fair can feel complicated. {idea}Notice the heart of it: does my gain come from someone else's desperation?{/idea} Umar himself said some types of riba were not clear to him. Ask people of knowledge, and take the door the verse leaves open.
old: Money is money; how it grows is just business.
new: How my money grows matters to Allah, and there is always a way back for whoever turns.
try: Look at one of your financial dealings honestly, and ask someone knowledgeable one question about it.

title: Allah drains what riba gathers and grows what charity gives.
subtitle: The hidden arithmetic of money
then: Ibn Mas'ud said riba {trap}ends up with less, even if it was a lot{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever gives even a date from honest earnings, {reward}Allah takes it in His right hand and raises it, as one raises a foal, until it is like a mountain{/reward}.
now: The account keeps growing, but somehow there is never any peace in the house. Meanwhile the family who give from a small income always seem to have enough. {idea}Barakah does not show up on a statement.{/idea}
old: Giving shrinks my money and clever deals make it grow.
new: Allah removes the blessing from unjust gain and grows a single honest date into a mountain.
try: Give the value of a date from honest money today and picture it growing.

title: Faith, good deeds, prayer, zakah: and then no fear.
subtitle: The steady life set beside the anxious chase
then: Between the verses on riba, Allah sets a contrast. Ibn Kathir says the riba-taker is {trap}not satisfied with the pure provision Allah gave{/trap}. Then come those who believe, are kind to creation, pray and give: {reward}their reward is with their Lord, no fear, no grief{/reward}.
now: You lie awake doing sums, chasing the next side hustle, refreshing the crypto app. {idea}The verse offers a different kind of security.{/idea} Pray on time, give what is due, be kind. Let that be the floor under you.
old: I will feel safe once I have enough money.
new: Faith, prayer and giving are the real safety net, here and on the Day.
try: Check that your zakah or regular giving is up to date, and pray your next prayer on time.

title: Let go of what is still owed in riba, if you believe.
subtitle: Walking away from money you were counting on
then: Zayd bin Aslam and others said Thaqif demanded old riba from Banu al-Mughirah after both became Muslim. Banu al-Mughirah said: {idea}we do not pay riba in Islam{/idea}. The governor of Makkah wrote to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse came. They said: {reward}we repent to Allah and abandon what is left{/reward}.
now: Money you were promised, money you had already planned to spend. {trap}Letting it go feels like losing.{/trap} The verse asks for taqwa exactly there, at the point where it costs you something real.
old: Giving up money I am entitled to is just foolish.
new: Leaving unjust gain behind for Allah is what faith looks like when it costs me.
try: Name one gain you suspect is not clean. Ask someone with knowledge how to make it right.

title: Keep your capital. Do no wrong, and suffer no wrong.
subtitle: A fair deal that cuts both ways
then: The warning is the starkest in the passage: {trap}a war from Allah and His Messenger{/trap}. Yet the door stays open: {reward}if you repent, your capital is yours{/reward}. At the Farewell Hajj the Prophet ﷺ cancelled old riba, starting with his own uncle al-Abbas's: {idea}you take back your capital, wronging no one and not wronged{/idea}.
now: You are afraid that turning back means losing everything you built. {reward}It does not.{/reward} The verse protects you as well as the other person: you keep what is fairly yours. Repentance is not ruin.
old: If I try to fix this, I will lose everything.
new: Allah lets me keep what is fairly mine; only the injustice has to go.
try: Write down one step you could take this month toward cleaner money.

title: If they are struggling, give them time. Forgiving it is better.
subtitle: Mercy toward the person who owes you

key.label: What to do with a struggling debtor

then: Before Islam, a lender would say at the deadline: {trap}pay now or the debt grows{/trap}. Abu Qatadah found a man hiding from him over a debt. When the man said he truly had nothing, {reward}Abu Qatadah wept{/reward} and recalled the Prophet ﷺ: whoever gives his debtor time or forgives him {reward}will be in the shade of the Throne{/reward}.
now: Your friend still owes you from last year. He avoids your calls. You could post about it in the group chat. {idea}Or you could ask, are you really struggling?{/idea} And if he is, give him time, or let it go.
old: If someone owes me, I have every right to keep pushing.
new: Giving a struggling person time is charity, and forgiving the debt is even better.
try: Message someone who owes you and tell them to take the time they need.

title: Fear the Day you are returned to Allah and paid in full.
subtitle: Every deal ends in front of Him
then: This verse closes the passage on riba and debts. After {trap}war against those who persist{/trap} and {reward}mercy for the struggling debtor{/reward}, Allah turns every reader to one Day: each soul is returned to Him and paid for what it earned, and {idea}no one is treated unjustly{/idea}.
now: The invoice you padded a little. The deposit you kept from a tenant. The debt you forgave quietly. {idea}All of it reaches the same final desk.{/idea} Nothing is lost, nothing is inflated.
old: Once a deal is done, it is done.
new: Every deal I make will be settled again, fairly, before Allah.
try: Settle one small unfinished money matter today, fairly.

title: The longest verse in the Qur'an asks you to write debts down.
subtitle: Writing it down protects the friendship
then: Ibn Kathir calls this {idea}the longest verse in the Qur'an{/idea}. It came to people in Madinah dealing in loans and advance sales. Writing is {idea}more just, stronger as evidence, and nearer to preventing doubt{/idea}. He says writing for someone who cannot is {reward}a kind of charity{/reward}, as Allah taught the writer.
now: You lend your cousin a few hundred. No note, no date. A year later you each remember it differently and Eid is awkward. {idea}A two-line message with the amount and the date would have saved the relationship.{/idea}
old: Writing down a loan to family shows I do not trust them.
new: Writing it down is an act of justice that protects both of us and our bond.
try: Write down, with the date, any money you currently owe or are owed.

title: If you are trusted, honor it. Do not hide the truth.
subtitle: Trust and testimony when no paper exists

row.title: not my business
sub: I will keep out of it

then: Anas reported that the Prophet ﷺ died with {reward}his shield pledged to a Jewish man of Madinah for barley for his family{/reward}. When people trust each other without paper, the one trusted must return it. Ibn Abbas said hiding true testimony is like false testimony, and the verse says {trap}his heart is sinful{/trap}.
now: Your friend left her laptop with you. Your colleague asked you to hold the petty cash. You saw what really happened in the car park. {idea}The trust is yours to keep, and the truth is yours to tell.{/idea}
old: If nothing is written, I am not really accountable.
new: Trust without paper is still a trust, and Allah knows what I saw.
try: Return one thing you borrowed, or keep one promise you were trusted with, today.

title: Whatever you show or hide in yourself, Allah knows it.
subtitle: The verse that brought the Companions to their knees
then: Abu Hurayrah said when this verse came, {trap}the Companions fell to their knees: we cannot bear this{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ said: do not say we hear and disobey; say {reward}we hear and obey, Your forgiveness, our Lord{/reward}. When they said it, Allah sent the next two verses.
now: Thoughts you are ashamed of. Envy you would never say aloud. Intrusive thoughts at prayer. {idea}You cannot hide them from Allah.{/idea} The Companions felt that weight too, and the answer was to turn toward Him, not away.
old: My inner thoughts are completely private.
new: Allah sees inside me, so I bring all of it to Him and say: we hear and obey.
try: When an ugly thought passes today, say: Ghufranaka Rabbana, Your forgiveness, our Lord.

title: We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord.
subtitle: The answer the Companions gave, now part of the Qur'an
then: The words the Companions spoke in fear became {reward}verses of the Qur'an{/reward}. On the Night Journey the Prophet ﷺ was given {reward}the five prayers and these last verses of Al-Baqarah{/reward}. He said whoever recites the last two verses at night, {idea}they will suffice him{/idea}.
now: A hard instruction lands: in a hadith, a khutbah, your own conscience. You feel the urge to argue it away. {idea}Try their words instead: I hear, I obey, forgive me where I fall short.{/idea}
old: I will accept the parts of faith that feel easy.
new: I believe in all of it and answer like the Companions: we hear, we obey, forgive us.
try: Recite the last two verses of Al-Baqarah tonight before you sleep.

title: Allah never asks more than you can carry. Then ask Him.
subtitle: Every line of this dua was answered: I have done so
then: After the Companions said we hear and obey, Allah sent this verse. Muslim records that after {reward}each line of the dua, Allah said: I have done so{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says {idea}passing thoughts one cannot control are not punished{/idea}, and disliking evil thoughts is itself part of faith. The Prophet ﷺ said: I was sent with the easy, upright way.
now: The exam you failed despite studying. The prayer you forgot. The burden that feels too heavy at 2am. {reward}Allah knows your limit better than you do, and He set it.{/reward} The surah ends by putting this dua in your mouth.
old: I am being crushed by more than I can handle.
new: Allah does not burden me beyond my capacity, and He has promised to answer this dua.
try: Memorize the final dua of Al-Baqarah, one line a day, starting with Rabbana la tu'akhidhna.
